speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to table P.C. 3205, of May 31, 1943, an order in council defining the conditions under which members of the armed forces may participate in political matters. As this order has reference to members of parliament and will be of interest to them I believe it should be tabled forthwith.

On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ORDER IN COUNCIL WITH RESPECT TO PARTICIPATION IN POLITICAL MATTERS
speechtext:
I desire [DOT] to address a question to the Prime Minister and to make a suggestion to him and to the three ministers representing the armed services. The question arises out of the order in council which has just been tabled, which is P.C. 3205, dated May 31. The recital in the order in council indicates that it is desirable to have uniformity of policy in respect of participation in political activities by members of the armed forces, and that would seem to indicate that there had not been uniformity in the past. The specific suggestion I have to make to the Prime Minister and to the three ministers is this, that there is a limitation of one month for a candidate preceding an election for the dominion or provincial house, or a by-election, and I suggest that this is not long enough. In the second place I suggest that the limitation of one month allowed to members of
the armed forces to attend parliament or the legislature in a given year is not sufficient. I hope this will be reviewed.

subtopic: LOWER ST. LAWRENCE REGION-APPOINTMENT OP DEFENCE COORDINATION OFFICER

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: LOWER ST. LAWRENCE REGION-APPOINTMENT OP DEFENCE COORDINATION OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the ministers of national defence having made their respective statements to the house on defence matters generally, this would appear to be an appropriate moment for me to make a statement with respect to measures which have been adopted, in cooperation with civilian authorities, in the organization of the defences of the lower St. Lawrence region, with a view more particularly to countering expected submarine activities in that area.
These measures include the appointment of a defence coordination officer to coordinate civilian defence efforts and provide the necessary liaison with the service forces in the region.
Upon the advice of the chiefs of staff, Vice-Admiral Percy Nelles, Air Marshal Lloyd S. Breadner, and Lieutenant-General Kenneth Stuart, the government has appointed Squadron Leader J. P. J. Desloges, R.C.A.F., as defence coordination officer in the Gaspe and lower St. Lawrence.
The creation of this new position and the appointment to it of Squadron Leader Desloges complete an extensive and highly integrated organization of all civilian and service defence facilities of this region. The service-civilian organization will be operative against any type of enemy action, but it has been designed particularly with a view to providing the most powerful possible countermeasures to German U-boat activities which are to be expected in the waters of the river and gulf this season.
Squadron Leader Desloges' duties will be to supervise and coordinate the work of the civilian organizations which will operate in intimate cooperation with the navy, army, and air force, and to provide liaison between these civilian organizations and the armed forces. The civilian organizations are the Quebec civilian protection, committee (AjR.P.), the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Quebec provincial police, and the aircraft detection corps. Partly in the civilian and partly in the service field, the reserve army also has an important role to play in the plan.
Specialized instruction in submarine detection and aircraft identification is being given

Defence-St. Lawrence
to the residents of eveiy town, village and hamlet of the Gaspe and lower St. Lawrence region, and also to all persons in the rural districts, including remotely located farmers, fishermen and lumbermen. Four mobile instruction units are already at work and to date more than thirty community meetings have been held. These meetings, which are for the purpose of forming local civilian defence organizations and for hearing details of the plan, have almost all been called by the municipal authorities themselves. In nearly every instance, they have been presided over by the parish priest or the' mayor. Speakers provided by the civilian protection committee, the aircraft detection corps, the local reserve army units, and by the other defence forces, have addressed these meetings, describing how each organization and service fits into the plan.
Briefly, the already smoothly working aircraft detection corps is being extended and trained to function equally well as a submarine detection corps. The aircraft detection corps, along with units of the Quebec civilian protection committee, will provide the means through which all citizens can render invaluable service. It need be no secret that members of the aircraft detection corps have already made valuable contributions in the battle against the U-boats, particularly off our Atlantic coasts, during the winter months.
At the present time members of the aircraft detection corps in the Gaspe and lower St. Lawrence region are turning in more than 500 reports of all kinds a week. Most of these reports have, of course, referred to the sighting of our own planes. The story of how members of the aircraft detection corps have facilitated the rescue of lost airmen is already well known.
This aircraft detection work has given a large organization excellent training and practice in handling reports swiftly. When a submarine is sighted this training, and the channels of communication already established, will enable a clear-cut report, devoid of the confusion of undue excitement, to reach operational units of the navy, army and air force in the shortest possible time.
To get action, any resident of the region who sights a submarine, or any aircraft detection corps observer who sights either an aircraft or a submarine, has only to go to the nearest telephone and ask the operator for "Aircraft Detection Corps". The operator will instantly clear all lines to a reporting centre connected with the operational units so that the persons reporting may give their messages directly to the service personnel who are on

duty at the reporting centre twenty-four hours a day. The reporting centre passes the information by direct telephone to the operational units of the defence services concerned where immediate action is taken in accordance with pre-arranged plans for dealing with the enemy.
A point which I wish to emphasize is that the report goes from the reporting centre directly to operational units which not only have full authority but the duty of taking instant action. Every officer knows exactly what has to be done and knows that it is his job to get it done without waiting for instructions from any higher authority. Furthermore, among the services plans have been so fully worked out that combined operations by- two or more of the services occur automatically without waiting for further instructions from higher authority.
Thus, the moment a report is received at an operational station, planes of the air force that are already in the air on anti-submarine patrol are directed by radio to the spot where the UJboat was sighted. Ships of the navy already on patrol in the same area are also directed by radio to the location. If the scene is one in which shore guns of the army can be effective, the appropriate battery is immediately notified and has full authority to go into instant action. Meanwhile other planes at aerodromes in the district and additional naval vessels at local harbours are in constant readiness.
After action orders have been given, or possibly simultaneously with them, reports of course go to superior authority. These are not only for the information of such authority but are also to enable senior officers to order into action, if they deem it necessary, any additional forces from neighbouring or perhaps distant districts which they think might add to the success of the operations, but let me again make it clear, in view of misconceptions on the part of some of the public last year, that a message does not go all the way to headquarters in Nova Scotia and orders come all the way back again before counter-action against the enemy is initiated.
In certain remote areas there are as yet no telephone lines. In these cases means are available for getting the messages through by telegraph. If neither telephone nor telegraph lines exist, radio communication is available. All operators, whether telephone, telegraph or radio, are already fully instructed in the means of getting messages through rapidly. An observer who spots a submarine in regions not served by phone can get his message through by getting it to any telegraph or radio operator. A further detail worth mentioning is that all three means of com-

Defence-St. Lawrence
munication will be available for emergency messages of this kind twenty-four hours a day. In districts where the rural telephone system, for example, has in the past closed - down during the night, special arrangements through the cooperation of all concerned have been made for operators to answer at any hour all incoming calls reporting aircraft movements or enemy activity.
It has been mentioned that the reserve army, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the Quebec provincial police, and the Quebec civilian protection committee, all have important roles in the over-all plan. The job of the reserve army is a dual one. All its members in the Gaspe and lower St. Lawrence region have been made ex officio members of the aircraft detection corps organization. In this capacity they will function along with all other civilians as submarine and aircraft spotters. If, however, local defensive action is required, the reserve army units are equipped and trained to defend their communities and put up effective resistance pending the arrival of additional military forces or assistance from the naval or air services.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Quebec provincial police will maintain a vigilant watch for possible enemy agents and saboteurs. They will be assisted by the reserve and active army units located at isolated points along the coast and by information furnished by members of the civilian defence organizations.
I should like to point out that bringing thousands of civilians into our defensive system in this region implies no weakening or relaxing of the defensive facilities already provided by the armed services. On the contrary, naval, land, and air defences undertaken by the active service forces have all been considerably strengthened during the winter months. What has happened in bringing civilian organizations into active participation to a much greater degree than formerly, is that the armed forces and police authorities are being provided with thousands of additional eyes and ears-and these extra eyes and ears are being given technical instructions to make them extremely useful. The navy, army, air force, and police will maintain their patrols as usual, but all four will now have the advantage of the additional help provided by all residents of the region.
Along with the community meetings which are being held in the Gaspe and lower St. Lawrence region by the mobile instruction units (these units, by the way, will use boat and plane if necessary to get to places not served by roads), the system of instruction of the civilian population includes the use of
pamphlets and posters and the cooperation of press and radio, The aircraft detection corps and the Quebec civilian protection committee are jointly responsible for the educational programme. This programme is planned to include aircraft detection corps exercises. In these exercises the residents of the various communities would have an opportunity to test their skill in aircraft recognition and their efficiency in making concise, clear reports. Other details which will be taken care of are educational work to make the "dim-out" in this region still more effective, and the civilian protection committee will explain to the citizens what this precautionary measure does and why it is necessary.
Another educational campaign that will be intensified is discouragement of careless talking about ship movements and military installations. The purpose of this, of course, is to keep the enemy from gaining any information useful to him.
The new defence coordination officer, Squadron Leader Desloges, whose headquarters will be in the Gaspe area, has not only had extensive experience in combat in this war, but is bilingual and has a personality which should make cooperation through him between all the participating organizations an easy matter.
Squadron Leader Desloges was a member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police prior to his appointment to a commission in the R.C.A.F. in October, 1937. He was one of the early Canadian pilots to participate in the battle of Britain. He was wounded, losing the sight of an eye, in August, 1940, thus being eliminated from further front-line combat duty. As the result of a series of lectures which he gave, after returning to Canada he became widely known throughout the province of Quebec. Subsequently he was appointed to the command of an air gunners' ground training school.
Another prominent personality in the plan is Marcel Gaboury, K.C., who is not only commissioner of the Quebec provincial police, but also head of the Quebec civilian protection committee, both of which organizations are components of the new defence plan. Commissioner Gaboury will supervise the educational campaign sponsored by the Quebec civilian protection committee and will be assisted by the public relations officers of the three services.
The services feel that this fine cooperation by civilians will enhance the value of the coordinated defence facilities which they had already set up jointly. I need hardly say that I thoroughly agree with them. We have here
Food Conjerence

an ideal example of civilians and service personnel working in complete cooperation and coordination in the defence of our nation.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ORGANIZATION AND FINANCING OF RECREATIONAL PROJECTS
speechtext: I would like to ask the Minister of Labour what progress has been made in the organization and financing of the programme of recreation for war workers. This is an enterprise designed to provide entertainment, exercise and recreation for Avar workers, and I understand that a community conference was held in Toronto not long ago at which plans were laid in this connection. This conference was attended by community organizations of Toronto, representatives of the provincial government and representatives of the Department of Labour. I understand that the Department of Labour gave certain assurances that contributions and help would be given to this programme, and with that understanding the citizens of Toronto have carried on. I am now told that they are in an embarrassing position because the work is being proceeded with under private subscription by certain individuals and cannot be long continued on this basis. I would like to know what progress is being made towards carrying out the understanding and putting this excellent work on its feet.

subtopic: ORGANIZATION AND FINANCING OF RECREATIONAL PROJECTS
speechtext:
What my hon. friend says is true; conferences were held in the cities of Toronto, Hamilton, London, Windsor and Brantford for the purpose of organizing

recreational facilities. On April 9 representatives of the' established community councils on recreation, labour organizations, churches, universities and national organizations directly interested in recreation conferred with officials of the Department of Labour. Representatives of the governments of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec also attended the conference.
This conference asked for leadership in recreational plans, stressing the need for additional personnel to provide leadership to and coordination of efforts already made. Representatives stated that the existing physical facilities should be fully utilized but the required additional workers and publicity should be paid for by funds provided by the federal and provincial governments, industry and the workers, according to some satisfactory agreement.
A full statement of the conference was submitted to the national selective service advisory board. This board advised that a recommendation be sent to his excellency in council that, under the authority of the War Measures Act and subject to the approval of the governor general in council, the Minister of Labour might enter into agreements with provinces or municipalities to provide recreational facilities for war workers; and further, that an immediate initial expenditure of $40,000 be appropriated for this purpose. This recommendation is now before council.
An approach will be made to the provinces and other parties concerned to negotiate agreements. A national officer for recreation to promote the work will be appointed. It should be pointed out that in the past the development of recreational projects has been the concern of community groups and organizations, and of management. Government participation in direction and control is a new venture and one that requires careful consideration. There is little precedence to help direct the planning. So far as possible essential needs should be met and if war conditions have imposed too heavy a burden upon the voluntary community organizations, every consideration will be given to proposals placed before the government.

speechtext:
Under the second heading, pay and allowances, which I was discussing last evening, I want to draw the attention of the minister to the conditions under which petty officers and men of the Canadian navy who are stationed in Newfoundland have to live. I am not speaking from personal knowledge, but I believe the information that has been furnished me is correct. I am informed that there are several hundred Canadian sailors stationed in Newfoundland. When they go ashore they are given a living allowance of SI .75 per day, out of which they have to pay for their board and lodgings. Living quarters are not obtainable at reasonable prices in Newfoundland; in fact it is very difficult to obtain them at all. If a vacancy does occur the prices quoted for a room are from $60 to $75 per month. One vacancy in a rooming house was available at $6 per week, but the room was poorly furnished; there were three beds in it which were already occupied by five sailors, and the only available accommodation was space in one of the double beds. As a consequence of the lack of rooming accommodation I am informed that our sailors are sleeping in sheds, trucks, coaches, attics or wherever else they can find accommodation. The sanitary conditions these men have to put up with are, I am informed, deplorable. In fact, in many cases there are practically no sanitary conditions available. The men are obliged to. eat either in the Y.M.C.A. or in what are described to me as dumps and dives. They pay from sixty to seventy-five cents per meal. The high cost of living can be readily understood, since there are duties on foods entering Newfoundland, there is no price control and. there is great inflation. The cost of living, my informant told me, was higher than in any country in which he had ever travelled.
It is quite impossible for our men to live properly under these conditions on $1.75 a day. The United States government provides in Newfoundland suitable barracks for the accommodation of its sailors. Our government has failed, I understand, up to the present time, to provide similar accommodation. My informant stated that the conditions were damnable, and that it was. a disgrace to our government and country that such conditions should exist. I ask the minister if he is familiar with the situation, and if steps are being taken to rectify it.

I am not prepared to say the editorial is referring to that particular aspect. The editorial goes on to say:
This is no oversight or accident. Here is a clear confirmation of what this newspaper has alleged time and again, that naval establishments are placed anywhere and everywhere except in New Brunswick. How does the Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, explain this evidently deliberate policy? It no longer astonishes, it disgusts as an example of discrimination the equal to which it would be hard to find.
It seems to me some explanation is due New Brunswick by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and also the Minister of Transport, as to why New Brunswick has been treated in this way. It is not surprising that the premier of New Brunswick, a supporter of the dominion government, said this in a statement he issued to the press on June 5 of last year:
I am sure that the people of New Brunswick will persist in doing their bit, but the sooner, however, the tactics of discrimination and favouritism are abandoned, the better.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
His words evidently fell on deaf ears. As one of the representatives in this house from New' Brunswick I join with the premier of that province-and, I may say, with the provincial leader of the opposition, who on more than one occasion has raised his voice about this matter, in protesting against this discrimination and favouritism. I agree with the Telegraph-Journal when it says it no longer astonishes but disgusts, as an example of discrimination the equal to which would be hard to find.
The return of April 19, to which I have referred, gives a further example of this discrimination. It sets out that the number of military personnel, male and female, serving in the army on March 31, last in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island was 30,000. In New Brunswick there were 10,000. It is not only in the armed services that this discrimination exists. A return tabled in this house, which appears as an addendum to Votes and Proceedings of March 22, is entitled, "Report on capital assistance to Canadian industries." This is compiled by the Department of Munitions and Supply and covers the period from the commencement of the war to December 31, 1942. It shows that the government has provided capital assistance to Canadian companies totalling $1,723,827,099, made up as follows:
Fixed capital	 $821,042,913
Working capital	 902,784,186
No details appear to be given for the working capital advanced to companies in New Brunswick, but of the fixed capital of $S21.042,913, New Brunswick received about [DOT]6 per cent, or $5,336,750.
New Brunswick can point with pride to the way in which her sons have voluntarily enlisted in all branches of the service. They have not shirked their duty. The province has provided its share of all war loans, and it was the first province to reach its objective in the last loan. As the premier has said, it will persist in doing its bit, but is it unfair or unreasonable to ask that it receive a fair share of the increased activities brought about by the war, and a fair share of the expenditures the government is making?
On Monday, May '31, a return was tabled in this house in reply to certain questions which I had placed on the order paper, being
sessional paper 124-B. This return sets out the fact that the government has spent for the construction of buildings and the purchase of lands and buildings from September 1, 1939, to March 31, 1943, in Nova Scotia a total of $29,997,000 and in New Brunswick a total of only $19,000. Nearly $30,000,000 in Nova Scotia, only $19,000 in New Brunswick. I had to check these figures twice before I could believe my eyes. There is a cartoonist whose work appears regularly in many Canadian papers under the heading, "Believe it or not." He brings to the attention of his readers matters that seem incredible but which nevertheless are true. If Mr. Ripley is looking for material for another cartoon he will find it in these figures. If the Telegraph-Journal wants further evidence to substantiate its statement that in naval matters New Brunswick has been definitely and intentionally cold-shouldered, it will find it in these figures.
On May 7 of last year the minister told us that $635,500 was being set aside for the erection of buildings and other necessary works at the port of Saint John. I have asked the minister how many of these buildings have been built. A year has passed and my understanding is that none of them have been erected. In consequence the navy at Saint John is obliged to carry on its operations at a great disadvantage. They are housed in what might be termed a rabbit warren, and have been forced to carry on training operations under considerable handicaps. I ask the minister now if contracts have been awarded for the erection of these buildings. What buildings, if any, have been contracted for? If contracts have been awarded, who are the contractors? What buildings are to be erected and what is the contract or estimated price in each case? If tenders have not been awarded, when will they be awarded? When will the work be started? When is it expected that the buildings will be finished?
Considerable information will have to be furnished in connection with these expenditures. The third item covers travel, transportation and freight. I referred to the breakdown which the minister gave us last year, and under the heading of travel and transportation the estimated expenditure was given as $2,585,000, whereas the actual expenditure has been $3,382,574. I would ask the minister: Are the officers and men of the navy provided with free transportation when they are granted leave? If not, what arrangements are made about the amounts which they may have to pay for transportation? When officers and men are on duty, either in the Mediterranean or on

If I might digress for a moment, I would ask the minister to tell us whether any steps have been taken to have the insurance principle, sometimes called the "incurred during service" principle, applied to the men of the navy who are killed, injured or incapacitated while serving in Canada or in her territorial waters, instead of the principle that came into force in 1941 known as the "attributable to service" principle. This matter was brought before the committee last May by one of the members for Halifax in what I thought was a very clear statement. He pointed out that if a man in the Canadian navy is killed outside the territorial waters of Canada his dependents are entitled to compensation, but if he is killed while in Canada his dependents will not necessarily obtain compensation; nor in case of injury or illness resulting in permanent disability will the man necessarily obtain a pension.

Mr. Chairman, on April 19 last, I entered a series of questions concerning navigation on the St. Lawrence on the orders of the day. For weeks, I awaited a reply from the minister. His answers are less than satisfactory. He speaks of airplane attacks directed against the enemy, while the question invariably under discussion dealt with submarine attacks. What protection was given to convoys by the government when over twenty ships were torpedoed in the St. Lawrence? The protection afforded, in addition to being inadequate, was certainly not perfectly organized. Those disasters were the result of unpardonable negligence on the part of the government. In reply to the above-mentioned questions, the minister makes a great deal of the shorter distances to support his claim that transportation by land is more advantageous than convoyed transportation along the St. Lawrence. In this whole matter, however, I fear that the railways are being favoured beyond all justification. They seem to control the situation in their own interest, and to the prejudice of the public. That point should be cleared up without further delay. Do you want any proof, Mr. Speaker? The net revenue of the Canadian National Railways, over the last four years, was as follows: 1939, $20,854,418; 1940, $45,007,412; 1941, $66,608,341; 1942, $85,000,000.
The increase in the revenue of this railway is easily seen. The same applies to the Canadian Pacific Railways.
True, the St. Lawrence has not altogether been closed to navigation, but the situation is not far from that point. A mortal blow has been dealt the seaports of the St. Lawrence, and the fine port of Montreal particularly. The shipping of munitions, supplies and materials of all sorts by rail from Montreal to Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick has resulted in over a million-dollar increase in the Canadian taxpayer's burden. This state of things is dishonest as well as unfortunate. Let us hear no more of those blinds as an excuse for the poor administration which time and again, for months and years past, has been brought to light. The same method is always used:	thoughts are concealed the
better to hide unmentionable intentions; words are uttered without point or the better to

War Appropriation-Naval Services
deceive the public. Therefore, the ports in the St. Lawrence and our navigation on that river will be ruined as a result of our participation in this war which I opposed, seconded by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, by an amendment objecting to this participation which threatens to carry all before it, our youth, our civil liberties, as was evidenced this afternoon, our natural resources, our commerce, our industry and even our agriculture.
To end my remarks, I shall read a letter written by an experienced pilot, Mr. Cyrille Pouliot, of Gros-Pin, Charlesbourg, Quebec:
The Editor of the Standard,
Montreal.
Dear Sir:
May I bring back to your attention the sound advice given to your valuable newspaper in an interview by an important British businessman, Mr. R. L. Holmes. This important interview was given to the Standard on October 13, 1934. Here are the words of Mr. Holmes:
"What you here in Canada must always remember is that the St. Lawrence is your front door, and when you block the front door no one can get in your house."
Mr. Holmes said that Canada would be like Siberia without the St. Lawrence.
Yes, sir, we have at our disposition this important water transport facility which since 1939 has been ousted by the railways and they have taken a place of vantage at the expense of the Canadian taxpayers.
Who is paying for all that? How much per ton from Montreal to Halifax or Saint John, New' Brunswick? These are important questions for our members of parliament to ask at the session.
Give Halifax and Saint John, New Brunswick, their importance during winter months, but let us take the advantage which the St. Lawrence offers of cheaper transportation and thus save millions of dollars. This war is already a heavy burden on the taxpayers; why make it worse?
The ports of the St. Lawrence are known for their efficiency. Montreal was quoted by Mr. Holmes as a first-class ocean port. Often we St. Lawrence pilots have listened to praise spoken by ocean ships' masters of the skilful work done by the stevedores of Montreal and their quick ways of loading ships, the honest agents, and not the least, good pilots. Praise to the St. Lawrence pilots was given by your valuable newspaper on September 8, 1923-"The St. Lawrence pilots famed for efficiency." The St. Lawrence pilots are known the world' over for their efficiency, et cetera.
The Canadian government and the engineering experts of the federal department of marine have contributed in making the St. Lawrence river safe for navigation and brought Montreal as a recommendable seaport. All this was done for cheaper transportation, shipping cargoes as far inland as possible. Now that we are learning that the submarines are going to operate the greatest battle this year, it would be advisable to sail ships as much as possible inland.
There is 800 miles from Montreal to Belle Isle. The entrance of the gulf, Cabot Strait,
has a width of 41 miles from Cape Ray to St. Paul and 11 miles from St. Paul island to Cape North-Cape Breton island.
The Strait of Belle Isle is 10J miles wide at Pt. Amour. It would be important to concentrate our patrol at the above mentioned entrances also using mines. The Strait of Belle Isle should be fortified, also Cape Ray, St. Paul island, Cape North, and the Gut of Canso.
Not only the Canadian shipment for England should be shipped from Montreal but also the American goods.

Saint
John, New Montreal Quebec N.B. York
Glasgow	2,695	2,552	2,706	2,997Liverpool ....	2,762	2,626	2,793	3,074
One-third of the distance to England can be sailed inland safely by guarding the three entrances and patrolling the gulf. The gulf of St. Lawrence as far as Saguenay river is one of the clearest waters in the world, and cold 45 degrees Fahrenheit.

speechtext:
As we listened to the statement of the minister yesterday unfolding the story of the Canadian navy and what it has accomplished, my thoughts went back to not so very many years ago, when there were amongst us a certain number of people who took their pleasure in deriding and scoffing at Canada's navy. They were ignorant people, in my opinion, who were not possessed of the facts. They argued in some instances that the money which was voted annually for the upkeep of Canada's navy would be better devoted in other directions. I do not know that they did very much harm. They were scoffers who delighted in scoffing. But there were amongst them, unfortunately, a certain number of public men, and they were more dangerous because they had an audience. I wonder whether now, looking back at their foolish judgments, they are hopeful that we have forgotten their utterances and that their future statements may be given more credence. For, suppose that their opinions had been heeded, suppose Canada had dismantled her ships and distributed her men in other directions, the minister certainly would not have been able to tell the story he told yesterday of what Canada's navy has attained. If that navy had not been in existence in September, 1939, he would have had to start from scratch; he wmuld not have been able to develop it as
3430	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
it has been developed, and it would not have been possible for it to play the considerable part which it has played in these war years.
Certainly the story which the minister unfolded brings no blush to our cheek. In part, the progress, the development, the expansion which has been made has been due to the painstaking work of the chief of the naval staff and the officers associated with him, who, in those discouraging years, were able to carry on despite the taunts which were levelled at Canada's little navy, and laid the foundation for the structure which has been erected. What was that foundation? That foundation was the outcome of plans 'which began to be developed after the great war, when Canada received from Great Britain a certain number of naval craft with which to start the Royal Canadian Navy. The plan was laid so that there should be a small, efficient, permanent force, supported by two reserves: the Royal Canadian Naval Reserve, filled with officers and men from the mercantile marine; and the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, distributed through its divisions all across Canada, and to which were attracted the young men who desired to follow the sea if war came. The plan was based on an efficient, small, permanent force which would be enlarged from those two sources, the mercantile members of which would have received their training at sea, and the volunteer reserve would be filled by men who received their training in the volunteer reserve.
So we see that the Canadian navy of to-day has been built on a plan which was laid after the great war. Had it not been for that plan we should not have been able to get a navy of the stature which wye have to-day. The essence of that plan was the efficiency of the permanent force. In order to attain efficiency Canada looked towards Great Britain for the assistance which the Royal Navy has been ready to give in the training of the young men of all the dominions who could go into its training courses with the young men of Britain and so receive that training and gain that experience by which we now benefit. After that training our young men went to sea in battleships and cruisers until they had served sufficient length of time to warrant their being passed on as acting sub-lieutenants . to the Greenwich courses, and having graduated in those stiff courses at Greenwich Hospital, they then were able to return to Canada for the first time and be used in Canada's ships and shore establishments.
At the time that Canada's navy was being derided there was, fortunately, a far stronger school of thought in Canada which reminded the people that Canada at least had an

expanding export trade, that in Canada's mind there was budding the idea of nationhood, that somebody would have to police these trade routes of the world, and that if Canada did not do so she should surely hang her head if she was not able to make plans necessary to take care of her commerce. That reasoning, mercifully for us to-day, was strengthened by the growth of public opinion, was kept alive by these establishments to which I have referred, scattered across Canada -the volunteer reserve-and to a smaller extent by the sea cadet corps, which are in a far stronger position to-day than they were.
The minister referred in one portion of his remarks to the four methods of entry of ratings into the Royal Canadian Navy. I trust that when we get to the question time the minister will elaborate those four methods, because I do not think they are properly understood. He referred to the first as being through the Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve, the second through the naval schools and bases, the third through the technical schools and universities, and the fourth through ships. What I do not follow about that statement is that those who come through into the navy by means of the three latter that I have referred to must pass on to the R.C.N.V.R. to receive the further training necessary. The efficacy of the training given by the permanent force has had the effect of enabling a very considerable number, running I would say into tens of thousands, of men passing through the volunteer reserve to receive the necessary training in the short time that has been available to enable them to man the ships which we have built.
The minister told of the tremendous increase in the number of ships, from 15 to 550. It has been no easy task to find officers, petty officers and men with sufficient training, with the little experience that time would permit, to man those ships, and it has been due to the benefits received from the plan that I have referred to, and the methods of training which have been evolved.
The minister did not refer to a matter which I think it would be well for him to explain in the course of the discussion, and that is the capital expenditures to government-owned and private companies for the purposes of the naval branch of the service. A return was brought down last year which indicated that the sum already expended was $80,487, and that the capital commitments were $283,959. That was up to a date last year, which I cannot recall; I have not the return before me at the moment. I should

War Appropriation-Naval Services
like the minister to bring these figures up to date and I should like him also to explain why it is necessary for the naval branch of national defence to make these expenditures direct, because in most other directions the needs of the navy have been supplied by indenting on munitions and supply, through whose hands capital assistance to the companies, whether government-owned or private, has passed.
The minister referred to the entry of ratings and explained the two methods of entry of commissioned officers. He referred also to the fact that in future we shall be able to look to the sea cadet corps as a nursery from which to draw. I should like the minister to explain whether, under the auspices of the navy-for the sea cadet corps now work in much closer connection with the navy than they did before-the age of leaving the sea cadet corps has been raised. Hitherto the age at which a cadet had to leave his corps was sixteen, and so far as I am aware the lowest age at which a lad is allowed to enlist in the volunteer reserve is seventeen and a half. I wonder what arrangements there may be to cover that overlap, because in the sea cadet corps there are usually found a certain number of lads who are extremely well adapted to the navy. Perhaps there is a call in the blood, perhaps there is a particular interest which has grown up from childhood, and it is not advisable that there should be any gap when the time comes for that lad to leave the corps and before he is able to be looked over for naval entry.
I do not understand from the minister's remarks whether there is still direct entry into the Royal Canadian Navy as there has been hitherto for boy seamen. It is true that in the years of peace the requirements of the Royal Canadian Navy of boy seamen were very small indeed, and I know from experience with sea cadet corps, with which I have been connected for a great many years, that there was very keen disappointment on the part of a lad who earnestly desired a sea life but who, with so small an entry, found it very difficult to make it. I should like to know whether there is still opportunity to receive boys, as they leave the corps, direct into the Royal Canadian Navy for training. I should like the minister also to explain what deductions are made at the source from the pay of both. ratings and warrant officers and commissioned officers.
I do not know under what circumstances, if any, the national defence tax is taken off, and I want to know what other deductions there may be for contributions to funds for
the benefit of the navy. For instance, is there anything in Canada comparable to the Royal Navy Benevolent Trust, a trust set up in Great Britain which receives, I believe, 5 government grant, contributions from the public and, I believe, contributions paid in by officers and men? Its purpose is to take care of those cases which may turn up from time to time of grievous accident to a man or his dependents-cases of sickness, operations, financial trouble suddenly occurring. I believe that after the great war it wets of great service indeed in assisting men to get reestablished, and I do not know whether in Canada we have anything comparable to that. The sailor in the navy of course comes under the pension act and receives what assistance is forthcoming in that regard; but if there is anything further than that to which a man or his dependents can turn I should like to hear more about it.
As the development of the navy has proceeded, Canada's worth has been recognized in the battle of the Atlantic, by giving command of this side of the Atlantic in the submarine war to Rear Admiral Murray, as described gby the minister. That to my mind is not only a very excellent recognition of the part that Canada has played in the fight in the Atlantic, but it also emphasizes the necessity for cooperative work between the navy and the air. Ten years ago exercises were planned to prepare for cooperational work. The work was terribly handicapped by the short supplies of those days. I should like the minister to describe to what extent that cooperational work has been carried on since the beginning of the war, and whether it is developing apace. He has referred to the squadrons w'hich have been set aside for purposes of cooperation in connection with the fight in the Atlantic, but to my mind he was not clear in his description of the command. Do those squadrons operate under the command of the commander in chief, Rear Admiral Murray, or is it a parallel operation with the naval chief and the air chief operating in close contact but not the one under the other? In the statement made by the Prime Minister this afternoon the same question arises in respect to the river and gulf of St. Lawrence. Is the squadron leader who has been appointed to take supreme charge in command of the naval forces with whom he will cooperate?
Then there is another matter in connection with entry. Will the minister explain to vrhat extent, if any, there are categories of entry into the navy. We know something of the categories in regard to enlistment in the army.

As to the navy, however, we do not know whether there is only acceptance or rejection; whether a man who just fails of acceptance in a fighting capacity, shall we say, can be used even though he may have som* slight disability, and whether that applies equally to the lower deck and to the executive officers. I would remind the committee that the assistance which the Royal Navy has always been ready to give in regard to training has not been confined to our young men when they first enter. As promotions come to our officers and petty officers there are further opportunities for those men to serve on ships of the Royal Navy and to take courses drawn UP by the Royal Navy, particularly in connection with those young men who specialize in gunnery, torpedo work, navigation, signals, or anything else. In that way we have been able to give the officers and petty officers and some men of the permanent force the training and experience they have required in order that they may again impart it to the volunteers coming from the two reserves.
There are many other questions which will arise in the discussion of this matter. I shall not proceed further at the moment, beyond calling to the minister's attention mhese few points on which I have asked for further information.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
As I listened yesterday to the presentation by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services I was impressed by the fact that he was relating to this committee a most important development in the history of our comparatively young country. Think of the facts as he told them to us. Canada now has some 550 warships, which number will be increased during the coming year by some 70 ships. Manning these ships, and taking care of the shore requirements, are some 60,000 young Canadians. To me this means that a nation such as ours cannot turn back in its path of destiny; and I believe the facts related by the minister will play an important part in the development of Canada into a powerful young nation.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, there was a time in the history of Canada when her ships sailed the seven seas; that was about the middle of the last century, the period known as the days of wood, wind and water. I like to read of our wonderfully self-sufficient forefathers in the maritimes who were equally capable in tilling the soil to produce the fruits of the earth; going into the forest, cutting down the trees and shaping the logs into lumber and using that lumber to build ships; sailing in those ships to carry on deep sea fishing and then journeying to every port
FMr. Stirling.]
in the world carrying the products of their farms, of the forests and the sea. Unfortunately, as we all know, the advent of steam spelled the doom of that particularly independent and self-sufficient era. I imagine to the people of the maritimes that change seemed to come slowly. However, that economic revolution, together with the railway development in the United States, became the determining fSctors that helped bring about confederation, which in turn has brought about the development of this dominion of which we are all so proud.
I believe that the present significant growth of our maritime strength marks another really important development in the history of this nation. Since that period of Canada's greatness-because Canada was comparatively great on the seas in the middle of the last century -we could not be described as a maritime nation. We all recall the heated discussion which took place in 1911 and 1912 as to what should be Canada's contribution to the commonwealth sea force. No doubt it now seems strange to the hon. members of this house that the discussion should have occurred, or that it should have been characterized by such heat. I cannot help but pay a tribute to the great leader of the Liberal party of that day, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who even then had a vision of Canada, within the commonwealth, becoming an independent, fully autonomous nation, friendly with all and in close partnership with the mother country, yet capable of assuming the rights and prerogatives of nationhood and all the responsibilities that must go with the assumption of those rights. So that what is happening to-day is in effect a tribute to the vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the policy that dictated his attitude toward the development of our young nation.
I have no desire to enter into the argument of sea power versus air power, let alone to attempt to settle this controversial question. History alone, I imagine, will decide the question; but notwithstanding that controversy let me say, as the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) has said, that the history of this war so far has shown that sea power is still a vital factor which will play an important part in the determination of the struggle in which we are now engaged. It will be remembered that Napoleon was unable to gain domination of the world because Britain in that day controlled the seas. Napoleon failed because of his inability to overcome Britain's naval strength and .command of the seas. Hitler has found and will continue to find that he, too, is unable to storm or to break down the barriers of

War Appropriation-Naval Services
that first bulwark of British defence, the sea power which has stood us in good stead throughout the ages.
When we think of the present war, and what sea power has contributed to the allied cause, we must admit that there would have been no embarkation at Dunkirk had Britain not possessed the ability to take the men out from that holocaust. < It is also easy to realize that the magnificent efforts of those few members of the Royal Air Force in those terrible days would have been in vain if Britain had not kept the north Atlantic lane open, so that the new world could carry to her the food and munitions of war which enabled her to continue the struggle.
What would have happened in Egypt; what would have happened to the Suez canal, had control of the seas not enabled us to carry to that vital field of battle not only the sinews of war but the men to use those sinews of war.
And so throughout the history of this war -in Libya and in North Africa. To-day, when we face a moment of great decision; when we are about to invade Europe itself, where would we be if we did not possess that overwhelmingly important factor, namely sea power, with which to support the armed forces we propose to send to that continent?
Therefore I think, without in any way depreciating or taking away from the army or air force the warm and well deserved praise that is their due, we should never forget the overwhelming, importance of this vital thing we designate as sea power.
Canada now has a very strong naval force. According to the figures given by the minister, Canada is now the third most powerful maritime country among the allied nations. That is a remarkable historical fact which must play an important part in the future growth and development of our country, and in its relationship to the world.
It will play a great part, too, when we come to the peace table. When I think of Canada's contribution through its army, its air force, its navy, its productive capacity, and through the immense supplies of food and war materials furnished the allied cause, I have a vision that Canada will come to the peace table as a fairly powerful voice; and more so because it is well recognized that Canada has not raised its army, developed its air force or its navy for purposes of aggrandizement, or for purposes of aggression or warfare, but for the very opposite. We have that potential strength to stand at the side of those who agree with us in developing a world in which there will be that degree of liberty and peace for which we are all striving.
I rise to-day because I come from what is possibly the most land-locked province in Canada. Sometimes I wonder if those who live down by the sea, in our coastal _ provinces, think that we have no interest in the magnificent creation of our Canadian navy. Of course the facts indicate that that is entirely wrong. These show that out of the 60,000 officers and ratings which go to make up naval personnel, almost forty per cent came from the four western provinces.
I read a discussion as to just what created the appeal in the minds of men from the prairies. One suggested that it was the love of the far-off seas. Another suggested that life on the prairies is so different from life on the sea, that the reason was to be found in the lure of strange places. I do not know the reason. Perhaps it is an atavistic trait gained from our forefathers who came from many lands, and many of whom undoubtedly dwelt near the sea.
I am delighted, however, to learn, both from the records and from conversations I have had with naval officers, of the splendid contribution made by our young men from f,he prairies. In some ways those vast prairies look like the great oceans. Our boys from the prairies have shown themselves to be first-class sailors, and I note that the official releases by the Royal Canadian Navy pay tribute to the splendid young men who have come from the prairie provinces, and who have directed their efforts to the navy.
I should like to place on record a brief dispatch setting out a deed of valour performed by one of the ships named after one of our western cities. I refer to the Regina, named after the capital city of my own province:
On a pitch-black night, tracer bullets exploding against steelwork and vivid Mediterranean phosphorescent wakes revealed the targets to gunners.
The submarine sprayed the corvette's forecastle, wheelhouse and bridge with steel and explosive bullets, hoping to kill the guns' crews and upper deck officers. By sheer luck, only one lad was grazed.
Zig-zagging in hot pursuit of the U-boat, Regina brought port and starboard light guns to bear successively on the raider's decks-the one side reloading as the other fired. The captain, navigator, first lieutenant, after-gun's crew and several others, of the submarine, were killed as they attempted to direct offensive action against the corvette and man their armament.
At the same time the corvette's four-inch gun's crew blasted their quarry at close range with heavy shells. Despite the zig-zagging of the ship their aim was good and their shells tore great gashes in the submarine's upper decks. One shell hit just at the base of the conning tower, tearing it loose from the deck of the submarine.
3434	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
Regina drew first blood and was in command of the situation from the beginning. As she closed, ready to ram, the Italians lost all stomach for fight. Great shouts of "my friend" and "comrade!" arose from the deck of the U-boat, and the fight was over. Regina turned the beam of a large signal lamp on the conning tower, and men were seen swarming out, hands high.
The submarine sank soon after.
That is a tale respecting one of our ships named after a prairie city. Among the personnel aboard that ship were men from every province in the dominion, my own city of Swift Current contributing one in the person of Mr. John Grant.
I am sure the opportunity which came to the Regina on that occasion in the Mediterranean is the opportunity which every vessel of His Majesty's fleet seeks. That is the opportunity they seek constantly, in order that they may contribute to the valorous history of our navy, wherever their work may foe.
In passing, may I pay tribute to the minister for adopting the idea of naming our corvettes and mine-sweepers after the towns and cities of the dominion. That procedure brings home in tangible form the identification of at least one ship to the city, town or village whose name that ship carries. I know in my own small city of Swift Current there is a personal relationship between that community and the craft that bears its name. I am certain that is true of all other cities, towns and villages, such as Kamsack, Moose Jaw, Melville, Battleford, et cetera, whose names have been chosen to designate ships of war. It seems to me that whoever thought of this idea performed a valuable service for the people of this country through linking them in a personal way with some of the things our armed forces are doing in the course of their duty. I am sure that the people of Saskatchewan, in common with the people of other provinces, take pride in the minister's story of the building up of the Canadian navy. As I have said, Saskatchewan is a land-locked province but it feels that it has a part to play in all that occurs in this great dominion. Nothing has been closer to our hearts than the valour and deeds of our Canadian navy.
I wish to close with one suggestion with reference to a matter which has been the cause of controversy in this country for some time.
I confess that until recently I had not formed a decided opinion about the adoption of a Canadian flag, but I must say that I think the time has come when, in justice to the immense contribution which Canada is making; in fairness to the dignity of this nation of ours and without the least suggestion of disrespect to
I Mr. Graham.]
our mother country; in fairness to all our ships; in fairness to our army which -has fought and will fight upon the battlefields of the world, and to our air forces, we should have a distinctive flag to symbolize this great country from which they sprang. I for one think the time is ripe-I believe the great majority of the people of Canada will agree-to -have a distinctive Canadian flag.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during his most interesting and well delivered speech yesterday, the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Macdonald) gave us some of the highlights of the services which are being rendered to the common cause by the Canadian navy. Personally I have no quarrel with the Canadian navy because there is much in it that deserves commendation, but I hold the view that we cannot get very far by patting ourselves on the back for everything we do. I believe it is proper and desirable for hon. members to point out to the minister and the committee the mistakes which are being made from time to time in an endeavour to overcome and correct them. The Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of October 21, 1942, contained an article which I should like to quote. I wish to refer briefly to some of the practices of discrimination shown by certain officers in the naval service. It is an unpleasant task for any member to rise in his place and refer to these incidents, but someone must do it. This article points out the narrow-mindedness of some of the men who hold important positions in the service of this country, and it is as follows: Navy willing to take men, Probationary sub-lieutenants will be accepted, says commanding officer
The commanding officer, Lieutenant-Commander C. A. E. White, H.M.C.S. Unicorn, announces that a limited number of applications will be accepted for entry into the naval service as probationary paymaster sub-lieutenants.
Preference will be given to candidates with university degrees and to qualified accountants. In addition, some experience in accountancy, law or commercial training is required. Those in administrative positions or those who have already demonstrated an ability to take charge are most suitable candidates.
Here is the pertinent part:
In addition to the above qualifications candidates must be between the ages of 18 and 45 and be of British origin.
All hon. members know that our Canadian citizenship is made up of peoples who have come from many different lands and who have adopted Canada as their country. I know of several instances where school chums who have attended university together de-

War Appropriation-Naval Services
cided to enlist in the navy, and the same thing applies to the army and the air force. When they were accepted, those with British names were eligible for officer material, whereas the others were left behind. This sort of thing in time of war is most undesirable. Surely there is no distinction drawn on the battlefield; surely no one cares about the origin of a Canadian soldier who is ready to give his life for Canada. Information about these cases leaks out only now and then, but the instances brought to my attention were so numerous that I was astounded.
In his speech last night the minister pointed out that the task ahead is still a great one. Why not then erase all these differences? Why bring up the racial origin of a Canadian who wants to serve his country? I should like the minister to answer some of these questions when I get through.
I wish to ask him this question:	What is
it that makes these men of non-British origin unfit for officer material? I should like to know, because scores of young men from my constituency are writing me that they want an opportunity to advance, but there is simply no possibility of it on account of this prejudice. This state of affairs is most regrettable in a time of war when we are fighting for our very existence, and a different policy should be adopted forthwith. It is true that the navy is a traditional British service. The British have naval traditions unequalled by any other nation in the world. At the same time I feel that we should accept for promotion those who are not of British origin, if they possess the requisite qualifications and physical standards. I think the time has come when Canada should once and for all erase at least some of these distinctions and fight for a common objective. No one has any choice in the matter of birth or racial origin.

do not want to interrupt my hon. friend, but he has repeatedly referred to an article in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix stating that recruits must be of British origin. speechtext:
I am glad the minister has made that statement and corrected what appeared in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix. I feel it should be the duty of the departmental officers to check up on statements of that kind and correct them as they appear. That was not done in this case. I have known many young men in the navy, army and air force who have at different times complained to me about this discrimination. That condition of affairs should not prevail, and I am bringing it to the attention of the committee so that it will not recur. I am glad to learn the minister's attitude because we must accept all Canadians, regardless of their origin, as Canadians, particularly when they offer their very lives for this country and the cause for which we are fighting. The diversity of racial origin in Canada should be a source of strength rather than a source of weakness if our people are treated aright. There is an inestimable amount of cultural wealth brought along by the various peoples who have come to this country.
In closing, I should like to refer to the remarks made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in introducing Doctor Benes, President of the Czechoslovak republic, to the members of the two houses of parliament the other day. The Prime Minister said:
May I say to Dr. Benes that we follow in our parliament the practice he followed as President of the League of Nations, and speak in either one of two official languages. I know, had time permitted, the President, as was the custom at the League of Nations, would have wished to repeat in French the address which he has just delivered in English. I would suggest, that one of the two gifted gentlemen who will express our thanks to Doctor Benes might take notice of the fact that we are a parliament which recognizes more than one language.
I was deeply impressed by that statement of the Prime Minister, who took pride in the fact that we express ourselves in more than one language in this country. I commend that spirit and attitude to the various defence departments in the task which lies ahead of them. Canadians, regardless of their origin, and I would include those who are not of British origin, have pulled their weight admirably in this war and we should be proud of them all.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I had not intended to take part in this debate, Mr. Chairman, but I have one or two suggestions to offer. First, may I suggest to the minister that in view of the acoustics it would be much easier to hear him if he would occupy a seat in the front row and sit a little further down the chamber.
The minister made a very good opening statement. I would remind him that for many
3436	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
years before the war started I had consistently urged upon this house rearmament and that we should be training from five to ten thousand naval men each year. We have the example of Gordon on the Nile in 1885. I had also urged for many years an empire shipbuilding policy, the extension of the navy, the building of a large merchant marine. When the agenda of the 1937 imperial conference was laid on the table of this house I urged that we should reopen and establish shipbuilding plants on the great lakes and the two ocean seaboards, and that we should be building merchant ships and all that kind of thing. I also urged that we should adopt the Jellico report regarding the Pacific and aid to the Singapore base.
I have no criticism except constructive to make of the department. I have never criticized, either in the two wars or between them, its personnel, the men who so ably carried on. Between the period of the two wars I did comment on the department not having given proper aid to the mother country in its great naval policy and shipbuilding policy, and also having allowed men who were faithfully serving us in the navy to put up with the conditions which then existed. We know what happened after the great war when Britain, on the urging of Canada, leading the dominions, threw away her defences and her friends and listened to the babble of the pacifists, and when his own predecessors treated the matter with some levity. However, that is all over. No doubt mistakes were made. Unfortunately the country and the house threw away its army, navy and air force and listened to the babble of the pacifists, with the result'that when another war came upon us we were not ready and had no fleet except the merchant marine.
Starting from scratch, Canada has made, I believe a very fine contribution to the naval effort. But there are some matters in which I am interested in a constructive way. I have no criticism to make of the present minister; in fact I never saw him until he entered the house on the other side of the chamber. I have no quarrel with him. Criticism is a tonic which stirs governments to action and it is the function of an opposition, provided that the criticism is of a constructive character and is founded on fact and not raised for political purposes. I am a Conservative and have never been anything else. I want fair play. In the report of my statement to this effect the other evening the word "not" was inserted in front of Conservative; I did not use it. As I say, it is the duty of an opposition to give con-

structive criticism. Since the war began I have many times brought before the committee and the house suggestions and proposals for the improvement of the conditions of those who serve this country on land, on the sea and in the air. One was a bill in 1939-40 to provide free fares for soldiers on embarkation leave; another to supply cheaper meals and berths on trains and refreshments at canteens; also to ensure better transportation for the forces on rail and ocean services; to provide a high cost of living bonus to all soldiers and dependents, and not this pin-money to which I referred in connection with the debate on the army estimates the other night, something which is given to some and not to others. The bonus which is known as a dependent's allowance for board is, in my opinion, mere charity. There should be a proper bonus extending to all branches of the forces.
Regarding the chaplain service. I cannot see the necessity of three chaplains, one for each service, in a camp like the Exhibition grounds at Toronto. I do not believe it was ever intended when the services were divided that there should be duplication and triplication along such lines.
I have also tried to offer constructive suggestions concerning conscientious objectors, alien enemies in the universities, a national system of insurance to provide protection during and after the war against want and unemployment. Incidentally the 50-mile limitation on bus travel is causing a great deal of inconvenience to our soldiers. There should be a reduction in prices in the canteens for such things as cigarettes, tobacco, soft drinks, sandwiches, coffee and tea.
The government should give some attention to correcting inequalities of pay. Last session the minister after an order was passed by the house for it three months before, went to some trouble to produce a blueprint which was laid on the table of the house. It revealed a considerable number of inequalities especially affecting the lower paid ranks, as regards pay, subsistence, and transportation. We had also, on this order for return, a blueprint covering the pay of the women's army, all the three forces. If Canada has a citizens' army there should be less inequality of treatment. Many of our best men voluntarily enlisted at the lowest rate, which was $1.30 or $1.25 a day, when many had been receiving, in civil life, ten to twelve times that a day. I believe it was even lower for the navy, but the variation has since been corrected. Nevertheless there is too much of a difference between the pay of the ordinary seaman and that allowed to

War Appropriation*-Naval Services
the higher ranks. War is war. I am not criticizing the women's army, whose personnel are no doubt entitled to what they get, but the comparison of their pay with that received by other branches shows that the men who enter the ranks of our citizens' army-army, air force and navy-are not being fairly treated.
When a person enters the army, the navy or the air force he loses his civilian status. There is no doubt about that: once you sign your attestation papers you lose your civilian status. Now, we are a civilian army as much as the men who enlisted in the American armies during the war between the north and the south, and they did not lose their civilian status. The enlisted man retains his civilian status in England, in Australia, in New Zealand, but he loses it in Canada, together with all his rights of protection based on the liberty of the subject. He cannot even write to his own member of parliament if he has a complaint to make. Some letters which members receive are opened. I had a letter opened the other day which was written to me by a good soldier who won the Military Cross. It was concerned purely with a departmental matter, but it was opened by the censor. I wish to object to that.
There should be civilian inquests all over Canada for all the forces. I found it a good thing in the last war, as I told the Minister of National Defence (Army) the other night. In 1917 conditions in the hospitals were not what they should have been; in fact in our district they practically had no hospital. They opened the old base hospital on Gerrard street, Toronto, for some of the forces, although as a hospital trustee, as mayor, I closed it because it was not good enough for civilians, and we remember there was a flu epidemic in 1917 and 1918 which took away many of our men. I contend that a man who joins the forces is entitled to all the protection which the civil law accords him. Dear knows, he has enough to put up with as it is.
