speechtext:
May I say to the minister that I, not the minister, am making this speech. He can make his own speech afterwards. He has the whole year to make speeches; we have just one opportunity, when his estimates are here, on the particular appropriation bill. I notice in connection with the debates in the British House of Commons that on the appropriation bill these questions are brought up which concern the three forces, and there is criticism of the gross mismanagement of the whole war. In any event I am just about through with this portion of my remarks.
In connection with summer uniforms, some get them and some do not. As regards the navy, I suggest that during the summer and winter there should be a better uniform for those men who walk around our streets. It is all very well for them to wear the ordinary uniform on board ship; no doubt that conforms to regulations and all that sort of thing. But there should be some improvement so far as training at home days are concerned.
This empire of ours came into being by the sea and it cannot exist without the sea. I believe that these vast expenditures which the minister brought down last night, nearly half a billion, while they are commendable as far as they go, do not represent the total com-
3438	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
mitments which we shall have to make in the course of time after the war to protect us from another war. It is my opinion that even after the war we shall require very large expenditures for the upkeep of a national empire fleet as a part of the contribution of Canada to peace and collective security. The mother country has to import twenty-five out of twenty-seven articles of raw materials she uses, and we know what sea power has stood for down the ages, and what it has meant in particular to Great Britain and the British empire. I am sure the minister would receive the support of the Canadian people if he took steps to ensure a strong navy for this dominion even after the war; because I do not believe for a moment that the Canadian people will tolerate again such a state of affairs of complete disarmament as existed at the time the war broke out. Right alone is not enough. Right plus might will be right in the future, and right plus might will be the policy of the British empire, which will continue as an empire for all time.
So far as the navy is concerned, I would point out two appropriate prayers in the Book of Common Prayer. There are three prayers which have to do with our ships at sea in time of war, daily and before a battle, and the Rubric directs that these prayers shall be used daily at sea for use in His Majesty's navy, to be read at sea by all officers and men. In one of them, officers and men pray that they may be a safeguard unto Our Most Sovereign Lord King George and his dominions, and a security for all persons sailing upon the seas on their lawful occasions. That is a most eloquent tribute to the navy. It is a definition of the work of the navy in this war, and it indicates that the navy has a function wider than that of mere national and imperial defence or war effort. It is binding on Canada, The ultimate object of those who so gloriously serve in the navy is the establishment and maintenance of law and order, justice in the world and freedom from tyranny, as these prayers indicate.
The sea power of the British empire is not an instrument of injury or tyranny, though the navy has been an instrument for the overthrow of tyranny. It has always defeated tyrants, and it is the one power which the axis powers fear most to-day. It does not seek dominion but is an influence for freedom and for the protection of all those who go on the seven seas to pursue, as the prayer 'so beautifully states, their lawful occasions. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, I suggest that it would not be out of place for that prayer to be read here daily, seeing what a splendid page our

officers and men have been writing in the history of Canada.
There is one question with regard to naval cadets which I wish to touch upon briefly. As everyone knows, this country excels in aquatic sports, but many of the rowing and canoe clubs, swimming and aquatic' associations, yacht clubs and so on, have been driven to the wall by the great war, the depression and this war in succession. I was at a regatta last Saturday, where a great many secondary schools of Toronto and York county were taking part at the Argonaut club in Toronto, of which I -was at one time president. I have always taken an interest in the secondary schools. I began to interest myself in this work when I was on the school board and later in connection with my activities in the aquatic clubs of the city, and harbour improvements, as chairman of the harbour board, and from my experience I have no hesitation in stating that we were wrong when we took the control of the cadet services away from the boards of education and school boards, public and separate, where it had been since confederation. There was a big parade in Toronto on Sunday, and I suggest that the minister and his department might very well cooperate with these agencies, the school -boards, in the advancement of cadet services.
I notice that in a great many newspapers there are reports indicating that members of parliament from various military districts across Canada have been invited weekly to join all parades of the forces, Toronto excepted, in order to find out for themselves how the money to pay for the army, the navy and the air force has been expended. Those of us who come from Toronto and district have never had any invitation since this war began, to attend a single event in connection with the army, the navy or the air force, to see how one cent has been spent. Personally I do not want an invitation because I have not the time to attend in any event; but I object to members of parliament being passed over in that way when they represent the people in federal affairs.
I cannot understand why it is that a statement was not given long ago of Canada's part in money and munitions as to the great armada to Algiers and Morocco. There has been no such statement on behalf of the government so far. Probably the government will make a statement later on. He gave us a very good account of the expansion of his department, and the statement he made last night contained a great deal of useful information which I did not have, and which I do not believe other members had. But I think we should have had

War Appropriation-Naval Services
long ago some sort of statement along the lines I suggest. Our military forces have written a glorious chapter in the story of the war so far; yet no one knows up to the present where Canada was in the desert victory, and it would be interesting to have a statement with regard to the part Canada played in North Africa in that connection.
I suggest also that it would be well to have a statement to clear up certain criticism that has been made with regard to the choice of barracks. As I said three years ago, with reference to the army and the other services, I could not understand then, any more than I can understand now, why certain camps were chosen in locations all over Canada for no military or strategic objective and where it was difficult to obtain water and sewers. I made inquiries in this connection at the session before last, and I was informed that it was the Minister of Munitions and Supply who had to do with the location of those camps. The navy has not as large a number as the other services, but in the choice of barracks in some of the large cities the minister, I am sure, has a great deal of difficulty in getting proper locations for the navy. He must find it difficult in Toronto. It is not very good advertising so far as I can see, although he has an excellent and popular real estate man in Lieutenant-Colonel Goodwin Gibson. In my opinion it is a wrong policy for us to have pages of advertisements in the newspapers displaying some large pictures of establishments like Sir Joseph Flavelle's house, one on Crescent road, and other mansions, when they are having such difficulties in housing the soldiers in the cities. There may be reasons for it which the minister can give; I do not know. Mind you, I am not criticizing the selection; I am simply calling attention to the policy, of our policy for certain of the forces, and no housing for soldiers' families.
I wish to encourage the department in its war effort. I am very much alarmed at what is going on in Canada. I do not like to see the apathy and political ignorance that prevail, as well as the false optimism. We seem to think the war is already won, and as I said the other day, red herrings are being drawn across the trail. You will hear throughout the country, in various public places, in the press, at public meetings and on the radio, suggestions to the effect that we have practically won the war already. Too many people in Canada seem to think there is a short-cut to victory, but there will be no short-cut to the winning of this war. There is no royal road to victory in this war, and we have no reason to expect
it as a matter of divine right. We have no right to expect that we shall win by divine right, as is preached from some of the pulpits. It is not going to be an easy task, I can tell you; it is going to become harder all the time. We are now in the very darkest hours of the whole war, and we cannot win except by methods of total war. This is a struggle for the survival of the fittest. The fact is that we must fight through this war to the end; that we must kill Germans, Japs and Italians, with no thought of quarter, or ourselves and our forces be killed. Until the issue is decided, that fact should be dwelt upon by all who speak with authority; we should allow no red herrings of social security to be drawn across the trail to obscure the real issue, for this is a matter of primary importance. There are some people in Canada who in their speeches over the radio and otherwise would lead us to believe that the war will be over soon. Some of our government agencies do the same thing. Our publicity departments repeat the same propaganda cries: "This war is different from the last war", and tell us that non-essential and unimportant things are to play a decisive role. We must remember that the non-military things are secondary. War is war, and these should be faced as primary matters.
We are told that we are not fighting the German people at all, but only a lot of German dictators; we hear about propaganda successes; we are told of the stranglehold of the blockade and things of that kind. Over one and three-quarters million Germans have been killed so far in this war, but the German people as a whole support their leaders 100 per cent and have not changed one bit. In spite of all the damage that has been done by the air force, there is no doubt that we must regain command of the seas before we can embark upon a very large peninsular war, which will have to come before this war is won. No doubt the blockade is a major irritant, but in my opinion it never will be a deciding factor in this war.
There are one or two other matters to which I wish to refer. I do not think enough attention has been paid to the matter of records of the forces in this war. Why, in regard to the navy, the army and the air force we cannot tell to-day how many men have enlisted from any given municipality. The other day the navy minister gave a very fair statement in regard to the chaplain service, but his figures were given in the aggregate; there were no percentages as given by the air and army. When the war is over,



War Appropriation-Naval Services
how is a municipality to know what men enlisted there; how is Hamilton or London or Toronto to know? These men in the forces from our cities are enlisting right across Canada. In connection with the victory loan we are told every day how much has been subscribed by each and every municipality in the smaller places throughout the country, but apparently we have no records in connection with enlistments. We can do a great deal to improve the matter of our records. The ministers tell us that it would be necessary to go over all the attestation papers to obtain this information. If that is so, it seems a queer system, a relic of the seven years' war; here we are spending over five billion dollars a year and we cannot tell how many men have enlisted from the various localities I have mentioned, or their names.
Then I fail to see why we should have all these press officers in the three war departments. I do not understand why one or two press officers could not handle all the work in cities like Hamilton and Toronto. I do not understand the reason for the large expenditures and these duplications that have been made in this connection. Yesterday the navy minister covered a great deal of ground in his remarks, and now I find a connection with the other services. Since this war began, there has been dual control as between the civil service commission and the various war departments. For example a return shows that in the air force 5,946 officers were appointed without having worn a uniform previously; they were just glorified civilians. I do not know the figures for the navy. Of course it is a newer organization, and I admit that a great deal of credit must be given for what has so far been accomplished. I believe, however, some solution should be found of this problem. I have another return showing that in the air force in the huts on our waterfront three or four hundred people were brought here from all over Canada, carpenters and all sorts of people, without the civil service commission knowing anything about the matter.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would
have concluded my moderate remarks before six o'clock, had it not been for the unnecessary interruptions of the minister. May I say regarding him, as I said before, that I have no objection to his department; far from it. I

will say this, that before he came into the house I had been a warm supporter of this department, and of rearmament. I never criticized the personnel, or anything like that, at all.
However, I may say that he interrupted me. I was a former chairman of the Toronto harbour board, and it was during that time that the work was begun and completed on the whole waterfront. In addition to that, during the last war, as chairman of the board of police commissioners I insisted on civilian inquests into cases of deaths of soldiers in training in that city, for the protection of the soldiers on land, on sea and in the air, and with good results for recruiting and for the protection of civilian rights in our citizens' army during that war and since.
During the debate to-day the minister asked me if I was aware of what is being done in Britain. I certainly am. I was aware long before he came into the house-about eighteen years before he came to the House of Commons-of what is and was being done on land, sea and in the air in all our empire in this and the last war regarding protection for the soldiers; and I do not need a lecture from him in that connection.
I may say that since the war started I have had on the order paper a resolution for the better care and protection of soldiers, and men in the navy and other branches of the service. I have no personal quarrel with the minister or anyone else. I am told he is a very likeable personality. I do not know him very well. But that is what I have been told, and I believe it. But I will point out to him that, in connection with his department and this matter, I have had on the order paper since the war started a resolution for soldier protection, as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should immediately consider the advisability and urgent necessity of adopting improved measures for the better protection of all soldiers who serve in His Majesty's forces and more particularly-(a) that a system of life insurance on all soldiers be established to include provision for their dependents both during and after the war; (b) that a daily allowance be made for local car fare and for free fares on Canada's railways under the Railway Act (R.S.C.);	(c) provision for a
revision and improvement in rates of pay, subsistence and other allowances of all ranks, especially privates and non-commissioned officers and removal of existing inequality between all classes; (d) a high cost of living bonus be paid to all dependents of soldiers adjusted from time to time to include better allowances for all their children; (e) provision for a moratorium from foreclosure, eviction and certain other immunities from debt while absent on war duties and for six months after the war, and more adequate and improved housing for themselves and their families.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
The minister is an old soldier, himself; there is no doubt about it. He has had more experience in war than I ever had-unfortunately, and through no fault of mine. But during the last war, and when this one broke out I proposed that a system of life insurance on all soldiers should be established, to include provision for their dependents both during and after the war. The hon. member for Davenport was kind enough when speaking the other night to refer to this fact, and also to many other soldier matters I had introduced into the house since the war first began. I am asking that a daily allowance be made for local carfare, and for free fares on Canada's railways. When I was mayor of Toronto the street railway was not publicly owned, but we persuaded the privately owned system to give free transportation to the soldiers in our city. That is done in many cities in the United States, including Detroit and others. It should be done in Canada.
Then, there should be free fares on the railways. Why not? A return brought down shows that the two railways in Canada made more money out of this war to the end of 1940 -a year and three months-than they made out of the whole four years of the last war, and two years thereafter. Is there any reason why the people of Canada, who own the national railways, should charge soldiers' families $2.05 to go from Camp Borden on a visit to our soldiers, and $1.05 for each child, or over a week's pay?
The other provision I have urged in the house is that provision be made for a revision and improvements in rates of pay, subsistence and other allowances for all ranks, especially privates, and non-commissioned officers, and the removal of existing inequalities between all classes. I have urged, too, that a high cost of living bonus be paid to all dependents of soldiers, to be adjusted from time to time to include better allowances for all their children. Then I have urged that provision be made for a moratorium.
They talk about the Sparkman act! I have correspondence with these various gentlemen at Washington. Some of them came to Toronto in 1940 and saw the late Mr. Thomas Bradshaw and myself about this matter. But the only hon. member who has been kind enough to refer to it was the hon. member for Davenport. We adopted that system, in Toronto during the last war. I must admit that three of the defence ministers wrote me letters. The Minister of Pensions and National Health, who has taken a great deal of interest in this subject, wrote a letter, as did the minister for the army, and the ministers for the air force and navy. I might say that the
three of them wrote very fine letters to me, after I had sent copies of the act to them, away back last fall, and said most of the provinces had in part Sparkman acts in the last war. We have had this system in Toronto, as the Minister of Pensions and National Health knows, in the last war, in insurance and other protection.
At the time of the last war many of the provinces passed legislation similar to the Sparkman Act, having to do with debts, mora-toria and foreclosures. I asked in this resolution for a provision for a moratorium from foreclosure, eviction and certain other immunities from debt while men were absent on war duties, and for six months after the war, and more adequate and improved housing for soldiers and their families.
The minister, who was at one time premier of Nova Scotia, had legislation of that kind in the last war. He is a soldier. I appeal to him to-night, as a minister, to see if we cannot do something about getting a better Sparkman act for all Canada. That legislation was copied in the United States mostly from Canada; the provinces and municipalities had it.
Yesterday the minister referred to the U-boat menace. I am glad to see that the situation in that respect in the Atlantic has improved. I believe it was in 1937, 1938 and 1939 I read in the house a statement of what U-boats had done during the last war. At that time I pointed out the number of sinkings there had been. We nearly lost the last war on account of the situation in the Atlantic. I know something about it, because I was head of a municipality which sent 55,000 soldiers to war. Some of them were on ships that were attacked. At that time the hon. member for Davenport was president of the British Imperial Association in the Earlscourt division, one which sent so many people to that war.
I urged in 1937 and 1938, sitting where the hon. member for Lake Centre sits now, that something be done to solve the question of an empire shipbuilding policy. I urged rearmament and the opening up of all our shipbuilding plants and an all-empire shipping policy for the imperial conference of 1937. I predicted what would happen in this war, and pointed out that Great Britain had more mouths to feed by five million than in 1914 and had fewer ships than she had in 1914. I gave warning of the grave peril and danger we were in. I also have copies of many pages of British newspapers, including the Times and many other papers, showing where
3442	COMMONS
War Appropriation-Naval Services
ships were sold in Great Britain, including men-of-war and others, for death duties and taxes, or for as little as $50,000.
I call the attention of the committee to the great lakes, and to the Welland canal along which I counted sixty-four ships tied up, with nothing to do. I prophesied the disarmament disaster to come from our pacifism, lack of shipping and all that kind of thing, and called attention to the U-boat menace. The Pacific question has been mentioned before in the house, but for many years I saw the grave danger in the Pacific. In the debates here from 1937 to 1939 I urged the importance of the Pacific to this dominion, and to other countries in the empire, because there can be no such thing as collective security until this war is won. And I can tell you this, I saw Britain and her dominions not only throw away her defences, but also throw away her friends, and to-day we are facing a very powerful enemy-Japan. She has a first-class navy, and always did have.
Without going into a discussion of what has been done, I urged dealing with the grave Pacific situation. The Minister of Pensions and National Health, who was in charge of naval affairs at one time, brought down very moderate estimates. That was done in 1936 and 1937, but he was not supported by some of his own followers in the house. He was right, and I supported him then and always as far as he went. Probably he did not go far enough, but I supported him at any rate. I would say now that in the Pacific we deserve what we get. We refused to face the situation, with the result, as the minister has said, that he had to start off from scratch.
I have nothing further to say, except to mention the explanatory note in connection with my amendment to the Railway Act for free fares, which has been before the house since the war started, and the abolition of the 50-mile bus rule for soldiers. The purpose of the bill is to amend the Railway Act to provide that members of the forces, when in uniform, may be carried free on railway trains within Canada. The same principle as stated therein was set out in a resolution during the first month of the war.
In the last war the railways voluntarily carried men for single fare on week-ends. Now they carry them every day at half rate. The Railway Act does not at present provide for any special concessions to soldiers during the war, nor has the board of transport commissioners power to order it. In view of the fact that so many camps are far away from railways and the distribution of troops for training spread all over Canada, it is desirable

to give soldiers some form of free transportation, because a large number have been killed on highways thumbing a ride in many places in Canada while in training.

speechtext:
I shall have some questions to ask and some general remarks to make when the details are before the committee, but I rise now principally to express my appreciation as one of the honorary presidents of the Navy League of Canada, Ontario division, for the generous remarks made last evening by the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services commending the navy league. I have been associated with the navy league for a long time. The predecessor of the present minister did not have the same opportunities as the minister has had, but he gave effective assistance to the navy league in the work it was carrying on. But, to my mind, the present minister has been far ahead of any other minister in his efforts to inculcate the spirit of the navy and the love of the sea into the young men of Canada. The results obtained through the navy league have been tremendous.
If my memory serves me aright, the minister said last evening that there were sixty-one navy league corps in Canada, and approximately 10,000 sea cadets in these corps. That is a tremendous advance over any previous time in the history of this country. I can remember in my own time when we did not have more than a dozen corps in operation. However, in those days there were some wonderful corps. Apart from Toronto, which always had a good corps, the Winnipeg corps, for example, was always considered a show corps. They were well trained, well led and did wonderful work. They were sent to many places to demonstrate what could be done.
Through the assistance of the minister the navy league has spread as it never did before. I believe there are some thirty corps in Ontario. I have a list of the names of these corps but, since it would take a little time to read, perhaps I may be permitted to place it on Hansard. It will be noticed that each corps is named after a fighting ship. For instance, the Belleville corps is named "The Quinte", and the Port Hope-Cobourg corps is named "The Skeena". I believe that those who read Hansard will be pleased to see that these famous names have been given to these sea cadet corps. On December 31, which is the date of the last report I have been able to get, there were 3,200 sea cadets in Ontario. I believe that by the end of the year there will be from 5,000 to 6,000. The Navy League of Canada has increased to a tremendous size. One might say that they are now in big business. Of course, this is largely the result of the war. They have done wonderful work. At Halifax, where the minister comes from, they have put up a recreation centre which is giving excellent service to the sailors and fighting men. They also have a hostel at which meals and rooms can be obtained, as well as supplies of writing paper and books, et cetera. These things have increased as a direct result of the support given by the minister, so that I am very happy to thank him for what he has done in this regard.
In Ontario there are sixty-seven branches in all, but they are not all corps. Practically all the larger towns and cities have corps. What do they do? The department send out instruction books on how to train the boys and give directions along the different lines of naval activity and merchant marine matters. I have just forgotten what the minister said last night, but he gave the number of the thousands of young men who had enlisted after having received training in different branches of the navy league. I am sure that the minister will support me when I say that the navy league has had a great deal to do with the enlistments in the naval service.
One would naturally expect a large number of enlistments from the maritime provinces, from the Pacific coast and also from Ontario and Quebec which are on considerable bodies
of water, and there have been. But the great surprise is the results obtained in the western provinces, particularly the land-locked provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta, in which there are no lakes of any size. They do have a magnificent river there, the Saskatchewan, which I hope to see improved some day. There are no lakes in the southern part of Saskatchewan, although there is one in the north. There is a fine corps in Regina which is well officered. This corps sends out speakers to different centres in the provinces, and I am sure the work they have been doing has done much to encourage enlisting.
While we expect boys from Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, British Columbia, Ontario and Quebec to do big things on the water because they have been brought up close to the water, the surprising thing is what has been done by boys from the prairies, many of whom hardly knew how to row a punt. They have blazoned the skies with the honour and glory of their names because of what they have done on the corvettes and torpedo boats to which they have been assigned. I understand that many of these boys are commanders, and I am sure that what they are doing is a great tribute to the work of the league.
The league has raised a lot of money by means of tag days. Of course this money is given by the people, but it is spent judiciously. I understand that expenditures are audited by government officials. The minister paid a tribute to the league, but I wish to pay a tribute to the men and women who have assisted in making the league what it is. The hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) is the principal officer of the Toronto-Riverdale corps. Here in Ottawa Mr. H. S. Southam and Mr. J. P. Kenny are president and vicepresident of the Ottawa corps. I shall not take the time to read the names of the members of the main committee in Toronto. The principal ones are the president, Mr. Gordon C. Leitch, a big businessman, who devotes a great deal of time to seeing that the work of the league is carried on successfully; L. T. Spalding, J. C. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we all
listened with great attention to the statement made by the minister last evening. That statement in conjunction with those made by the senior Minister of National Defence and the Minister of National Defence for Air outlined a record of achievement of which I think this house and the country may well be proud. The ministers concerned should feel gratified at the generous reception which their statements have received from the opposition side of the house. There has been, so far as I could observe, very little of what is generally called carping criticism. What criticism there has been has been of certain specific matters, and not at all directed to the whole programme which the ministers outlined.
The work of the navy of which the minister is head is not spectacular. Except when there are major naval engagements the navy is seldom heard of; its work is done quietly and unobtrusively. Nevertheless in this war it has performed a particularly essential service which has been of the greatest value. I felt myself from the time of the fall of France until the drive in North Africa began last November that the work done by the British and Canadian navies and the navies of the united nations had received perhaps less credit than to which they were entitled. The importance of their work was not properly understood or appreciated, and it was difficult to begin making comparisons between the work of the navies and the military effort of some of our allies for fear of creating disharmony and disunity in the ranks of the united nations. However, I think that phase is now passed. Personally I am glad at this time that I have no criticism to offer. I am not competent in the first instance to criticize the work of the minister, and, second, I am glad to say that I have had very few complaints so far as navy personnel and naval matters are concerned.
While we are justified in taking pride in what we have accomplished, we should be careful not to be carried away by these accomplishments but should realize that it was done under the stress of war. In other words, war became the country's great national purpose, and we allowed nothing, lack of money, lack of material or lack of anything else to interfere
IMr. MacNicol.]
with that one purpose. Consequently we have performed what we may call a great achievement.
But what I wish to call attention to particularly is that the navy was built for one purpose, namely the winning of the war. After the war is over, we cannot live and prosper by expanding or building greater additions to our navy. The high speed with which we built our great war machines for all our fighting forces should give us pause to think what our productive power will mean to us when the war is over. We should stop to ask ourselves how quickly we can build the capital equipment necessary for the greatest production of consumer goods that we can imagine. That, in my opinion, once we have achieved victory, is what we should be thinking of. I read in a British periodical not so very long ago that two-thirds of the important war instruments which now are part of the equipment of all branches of the fighting forces w'as not even conceived in the mind of man when the war began.
The hon. member for Swift Current said this afternoon that the greatness of our military power should give us an important voice at the peace conference when that event takes place. There were great powers at the last peace conference, but that did not mean that they could build an enduring peace. Therefore I would say that we have to bring more to a peace conference than merely great military power. The greater the military power we have, the more important it is that we have ideas and ideals, and determination to put them into effect, if we are to build a world in which young men will not in another decade or two have to give their lives in world war No. 3.
When the minister was making his statement last evening, my mind continually went back to the time when so many young men who are now in the navy, and who are now our heroes, could not get sufficient to eat or a place to lay their heads. Unless we take care, when this war is over, these young men, instead of receiving the rewards of their heroism, will be, as too many returned soldiers were after the last war, an embarrassment to the country nnd a nuisance to themselves. While complimenting the minister and the country on this great achievement of building an efficient naval machine, let us remember that this is not the end; it is only a beginning.

I think we can all join with the minister in the tribute he has paid to the shipbuilders who built the majority of the ships operating in the Canadian naval service to-day and built them substantially

War Appropriation-Naval Services
with Canadian, materials, and to the men and the officers and the ships they operate. We have some difficulty in appreciating the magnitude of what has been accomplished since this war began. I remember sitting here and listening to tremendous debates when we were determining whether or not we were spending too much in voting $30,000,000 a year for the army, the navy and the air service. I look back on those days with more amazement than comes to me as I hear the statements, by the ministers who have the responsibility of conducting this war, of the magnitude of the operations which they are still developing upon an expanding basis. I agree with the hon. member for Vancouver East that we should not lose sight of the fact that this war has disclosed the power which we as a people possess, and which, if properly used, will forever avert the return to the conditions of unemployment, poverty and misery which existed during the decade that preceded this war. I remember standing in my place in this chamber and saying to my colleagues, when I pleaded that we go on with any number of the millions of jobs for which there was crying need in this country, that if war ever came, the one thing we would find out was that we were not short of money. When you get a Scotsman as minister of naval defence, and he spends without batting an eye $489,000,000 on a naval service which was practically non-existent when he took office, in one year, you can fairly conclude that we were not short of money before he went to work and that certainly we have an abundance of reserves over and above the amount which he is spending. And, at that, he is getting only a small share of what we are spending-$489,000,000 for the navy, $4,600,000,000 for the army and the air force. Why, we were told, when we asked for a few million dollars to build some naval defences upon the Pacific coast and to maintain the nuclei of an army and an air force, that we were going beyond our means because we dared to spend $30,000,000. I hope the Canadian people will never forget this lesson or permit the government to forget it. "Where is the money coming from?" I used to hear. I hope we shall never hear that kind of nonsense again.
While I am on my feet may I draw attention to the fact that I was one of those who advocated the public ownership of the Bank of Canada, and I was told that that was heresy, and dangerous. I said that we ought to have our own bank and issue our own money. "Why", they said, "that is 'funny money'; you will wreck the economy of the nation." Do you know what we are doing to-day? We own the Bank of Canada;
we have a thousand million dollars of our own securities in that bank, and in exchange for those securities we have a thousand million dollars of Bank of Canada bills operating in this nation, unsecured by gold, and operating as debUfree money. A great many of my colleagues, apparently, are as yet unaware of that fact, because there are some other features which indicate that we have not yet come to realize that the power which is in that new technique is, after all, the basis of the power we are able to demonstrate in these reports from the ministers of national defence.
I wish to pay a tribute to the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, and to congratulate the government upon the selection of a man from the maritimes to administer our naval service during this war.
I often think I am one of the luckiest of men, because I happen to have been bom in Winnipeg; I was taken to the Pacific coast of Canada when I was less than a year old, and I had the privilege of living in the maritimes and getting some of the education which they dispense on that coast.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Our capacity to produce must be the measure of our capacity to distribute, and not our capacity to finance. Men must come before money.
And I offer this thought upon that issue: If we can spend five thousand million dollars on war; if we can give out of our goods and services the value of a thousand million dollars to England-which we did, and rightly, too-and distribute a thousand million dollars of war aid among our allies-and if that is not all the surplus we have, we should distribute more-then we ought to be able to do something better than 120 a month as an old-age pension for our own people of advanced age.
May I suggest to the minister that our naval service in the light of the achievements he has disclosed should be guaranteed against what happened after the last war. We want no post-war collapse in our naval or marine power this time. As a precaution against that possibility I suggest that we recast sections 7 and 8 of our Naval Service Act, and I offer this as a magna. charta for Canada's naval service, as a reward for the achievements the naval service has accomplished in the last four years, under its able minister. I would amend the Naval Service Act of 1910 by recasting sections 7 and 8 into the following sections:
It is necessary for the nation's defence and development of its foreign and domestic commerce that the Dominion of Canada shall have a naval service and merchant marine.
(a)	Sufficient to carry and protect its domestic waterborne commerce and a substantial portion of the waterborne export and import foreign commerce of the dominion, and to provide shipping service on all routes essential for maintaining the flow of such domestic and foreign waterborne commerce at all times,
(b)	capable of serving as a powerful arm of defence in time of war or national emergency,
(c)	owned and operated under the Canadian flag by the government and citizens of Canada, and
(d)	composed of the best-equipped, safest, and most suitable types of vessels, constructed and equipped in Canada from Canadian materials, in so far as may be practicable and manned with a trained and efficient citizen personnel.
It is hereby declared to be the policy of the Dominion of Canada to foster the development and encourage the maintenance of such a naval service and merchant marine.
7a. The minister shall have the control and management of all naval affairs, including the purchase, maintenance and repair of the ordnance, ammunition, arms, armouries, stores, munitions, and habiliments of war intended for the use of the naval service.
7b. The minister shall have the control and management including the construction, purchase, maintenance and repair, of naval establishments and of ships and other vessels for the naval service.
7c. The minister shall have and exercise such control and management including the design,
(Mr. McGeer.]
construction, aid to construction, purchase, maintenance and repair including operation and aid to operation of shipbuilding establishments and all ships and other vessels for the merchant marine as the Governor General in council may authorize from time to time.
What does that mean? It simply means that Canada must have ships, and have the best of ships. It means that the men in the mines of Nova Scotia, Ontario, British Columbia and other provinces will dig the metals and coal to build them. Others will drill for oil and cut the timber required. In a hundred cities and towns, men and women will form the plates, engines, gears and equipment and proudly build and launch them to their service on the sea.
Notwithstanding the fact that long since Canada has attained a ranking position among the leading maritime trading nations of the world, and has attained the position of fourth or fifth as a maritime trading nation, we allowed our merchant marine to disappear, and allowed our navy to die in its infancy from malnutrition.
Our Canadian boys were virtually denied the fulfilment of the dream that every British youngster has of some time sailing the seven seas under the flag of their own beloved land. But the seagoing career of the Canadian boy of the future should now be forever assured, from what has now been done under the farsighted naval policy of 1910. And we certainly on this side of the house should not forget that everything that has been achieved in the naval programme, which has been so ably prosecuted by the minister and his officers and men, has been achieved under the naval bill of 1910, which has hardly been amended since it was enacted.
Yes, the experience which we have had since 1910, and the achievements which we have accomplished have demonstrated what can be accomplished in the future. Of course other nations may be able to build cheaper ships. They may be able to man them and operate them cheaper; but we, by maintaining a policy of cooperation between the government and the merchant marine services, can maintain upon the seas the same high standard of wages and the same high standard of living that we maintain along with the United States upon this continent, for our people.
After the last war we made a feeble attempt to establish a merchant marine. We allowed it to die, because we could not make any money out of it. How much did it cost us to build what we had thrown away, when we needed it in the war? What kind of economy was that?

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Yes; Canadians can build a naval force with our own men out of our own materials. We can build a merchant marine, and we can go to work, produce and develop the cargoes. We can use Canadian dollars not only to take those cargoes to our shore lines, but to take them in our boats to the end of the line of distribution, and return. And if we do not do so, wTe shall find ourselves unable to compete in world trade with those nations which are going to do it.
Experience has taught us that as part of the British empire we must provide our own navy, and that we must provide part of the merchant marine which the empire requires. The magna charta for the Canadian navy I am now suggesting guarantees that we shall never again be short of naval strength or merchant marine service. In addition to that, if we carry out our policy, and prosecute it with the same intelligence and vigour with which we have prosecuted our war effort in this crisis, we shall find that "the wholesome seas are at our gates, our gates both east and west," is a message which will help us to go to work in the world with effectiveness when we stop fighting one another, and proceed to the business of feeding one another, on a better basis.
I congratulate the minister upon the magnificent work he has done since he took over his difficult office. While I appreciate the great work done by men of the army, I remember the days of the depression, when everyone was looking for a little bit of that $30,000,000 a year we were voting so hesitatingly. I remember when the present Minister of National War Services (Mr. LaFleche) was deputy minister of national defence and when men like Major General Stuart and Crerar, Worthington and Sanson were wondering whether they had made a terrible mistake by adopting the career of the professional soldier. But they carried on, and Canada's army is a tribute to the men of the permanent service who never lost faith in their careers.
I remember the air force when there were such men as Air Marshal Breadner, Johnson and Croil and a number of others who were carrying on under the inspiration of the work of Billy Bishop and other heroic Canadians who had left behind them a tradition upon which Canada's marvellous air force is riding the skies to-day. But there was another group. There was Rear Admiral Nelles, Admiral Jones, and Murray and Brodeur. Incidentally I may say that Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not the only great French-Canadian who participated in the introduction of the Naval
72537-219i
Service Act of 1910. The minister under whom it was introduced was the Hon. Mr. Brodeur, the father of the present naval attache of this country at Washington.
While the army maintained something of its strength; while it had the traditions of the last war; while the air force had the good fortune to be associated in the great British empire training scheme, our navy in this war travelled alone as a Canadian institution. Starting from scratch it has created a record upon its own bottoms, which I think is the proper naval term. Because of the ability which it has proven it made a contribution that has been a blessing to the cause of freedom throughout the world and has given to Canada a tradition that should ever make us true to the history of the people of both our great races, because both French-Canadians and Anglo-Canadians have always lived and thrived by and on the sea.
Let us never become canoe-minded again. Let us move forward and be true to our traditions, knowing that we are a great maritime power, that we are a two-ocean nation; with the arctic developing the way it is, are, may I say, a three-ocean nation. Let us not forget these lessons we have learned, and then there will be no need to fear poverty after the close of this war. We shall never need even to think that there ever will be misery and unemployment again in our land.

I should like to say just a brief word even though I was not born at Halifax, Vancouver or Winnipeg. I was bom and I am still living, for which I am thankful. I appreciated very much the introduction the minister gave to the work of his department. I thought it was well done. He did not have an Irish accent, but he had the next best. His address was not so technical that an ordinary man like myself could not understand it. As I listened to the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer), I quite realized why he was able to stand on his own feet and express himself as forcefully as he did. Through hearsay I heard something of his dad when I first came to Winnipeg in 1894. The hon. member is a son of a man who could take care of himself. He got a splendid start in life and I am sure that he is living up to the start that his dad gave him.
I agreed with him thoroughly when he described the times through which we went and how difficult it was to get money. I was serving in the branch of a church the officers of which gave me permission to allow men to enter the boiler room to sleep overnight. One winter we averaged seven a night, and

we did not always have to give them porridge and toast the next morning because many of them had left. I have no patience with the clergyman or with the member of parliament or with any Christian man who says one thing and does another. I should like to think that I shall be spared to live until after this war is over. If I am, I shall be just as keen' as any man in this house to see that fair play is done to every citizen of this country, that he will have a chance to earn his bread in an honest way. If he is not willing to work, then he will be put to work under other circumstances so that he may earn his keep.
The reason why I rose to speak to-night was the suggestion made by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Graham) about the naming of vessels after certain places. There is a corvette called the Fort William, and of course that is always music in my ears. The men and women of Fort William vied with each other to equip this boat and I never saw finer stuff given to any group of men. The crew appreciated it very much. I am hoping that some day the corvette Fort William will be able to equal in valour the corvette which was named after our sister city of Port Arthur.
The crew of that corvette must think always of the son of our Minister of Munitions and Supply-William Hastings Howe. He is an officer in the navy who distinguished himself, but who nearly lost his life in action. We people at the head of the lakes also think of what the Minister of Munitions and Supply went through himself. I am sure that quite often when he sits in comfort, has enough to eat and enough clothes to cover himself, he must feel chills running through his body in memory of that eight-hour ride on the open sea. I know the crew of the corvette Port Arthur must think of what nearly happened to the Minister of Munitions and Supply and what a loss it would have been to all Canada. They must think of the near call that both father and son had. They must remember when the minister's assistant, Gordon Scott, lost his life. With that memory in their minds I can see the crew of the Port Arthur jumping into their outfits when a submarine came within hailing distance and blowing it to Palestine.
We in Fort William have paid our respects in every possible way to the crew of the Port Arthur. It is an advantage to call a ship after a city or town. Of course, we at the head of the lakes think we are the hub of Canada, but other people may not think so. We think that our young men from the head of the lakes who have joined the navy are second to none. I

went over to the Port Arthur navy headquarters one day to see if there was an opportunity of a young man getting into the navy there and I found that four hundred local boys were already on the waiting list. I remember getting a letter from a boy who went over and he said, " Reverend Dan, we are just giving the enemy the same thing we said we would do for you when you were in the sub-box leading the hockey team. We give them everything we have." So that you can see what happened to that submarine when the Port Arthur struck it. The Port Arthur sent her sky-high.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am anxious to say a few words concerning the illuminating and remarkable report made yesterday by the minister for naval services. He has told us that our navy, which at the beginning of the war consisted of about fifteen ships, has attained the remarkable growth of now numbering five hundred, while the crew which numbered about 1,700 at the start of the war has grown to 60,000. The minister added, not without pride, that he expects that by the end of next year the numbers of our crew will be equal to those of the British navy at the beginning of the war.
Before going any further I wish to pay my compliments to the hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard upon his remarkable speech. In everything he said about the navy I am pleased to concur. The dream of Laurier is now realized through the energy and good administration of our distinguished minister for naval services. I am sure that if Laurier were still living he would be proud of him just as he would be proud of the Canadian nation to-day. I am proud myself of my country. If Canada had attained the position she enjoyed in foreign trade at the beginning of this war, it was due in large measure to the protection of the British navy on the seven seas of the world. Since we may claim to be an independent nation; according to the statute of Westminster; since we have now attained manhood, nationally speaking, I think it is our duty to see that we build according to the expectations of a sound and healthy people. The hon. minister in doing what he has done for our Canadian navy has accomplished deeds which will lead us to that realization.
It was a very good idea of the minister and his staff to give the names of our towns and counties to corvettes and other ships of our Canadian navy. I am pleased to mention, as the previous speaker, the hon. member for Fort William did, that a corvette has been named after the town and county

War Appropriation-Naval Services
of Chambly, which I have the honour to represent in this house. The corvette Chambly has accomplished many great deeds in the battle of the Atlantic. May I be allowed to mention one remarkable deed which the corvette Chambly accomplished in cooperation with the corvette Moose Jaw; that means that Quebec joined Saskatchewan in fighting the U-boat. They attacked a submarine and captured all its German crew. This heroic deed has been recognized and rewarded by granting to the commanding officer Prentiss the Distinguished Service Order of the British Empire. The men of our Canadian navy, it seems to me, have the real spirit of the men of the sea, as naval men are known the world over among nations whcse navies travel the sealanes of the world. They are humble men and consider they are just doing their ordinary duty in gallantly fighting the enemy in this war. To give an illustration, may I quote from a letter which my wife received from the commanding officer of the corvette Chambly, thanking her and the women of my constituency for what they have done for the crew of that ship. I quote in part:
I am sorry that we are not in a place where you and Mr. Dupuis could visit the Chambly corvette and see for yourself the ship named after your town and county. I am sure that you would be as proud of her as we are. We have a fine bunch of men manning her. I could not ask for a keener or a better crew in any way. Chambly has steamed many miles since she was commissioned, all of which time I have served in her. Her tasks have been many and varied, often arduous, as they w'ill continue to be till the war is won. We would not ask anything else.
I may be excused for having taken the time of the committee to recount these facts to hon. members from all across this country. Chambly corvette is only one ship of our Canadian navy; many other ships are fighting the good fight to-day and expecting, as this commanding officer says in his letter, to win the war, and, indeed, being sure they will win it. Such a spirit deserves, I believe, to be mentioned, and it is for this reason that I asked the privilege of saying a few words.

We have not been able to do it in St. John's, but we are making every effort to overtake that condition as far and as quickly as we can.
My hon. friend then went on to speak of the amount of money spent in Nova Scotia as compared with the amount spent in New Brunswick. He said that Nova Scotia had received a share out of all proportion to its share in Canada's war effort. I must say, Mr. Chairman, that I regret very much the practice of endeavouring to allot, war moneys according to sectional or provincial boundaries, without regard to the real merits and facts of the case. My hon. friend knows quite well, I am sure, that for nearly 200 years the city of Halifax has been a great naval base. It was established as a naval base by the British government in 1749, and ever since that time Halifax has been looked upon as the main British naval base or the main Canadian naval base, as time went on, in America.
The headquarters of the Canadian navy on the east coast have always been there, and it is only natural therefore that there should be a very considerable naval building programme in the city of Halifax in this war. It is also only natural that the outports near Halifax should receive some attention, because the matter of supervision is quite important, and it is much more convenient-to put it only on that ground-to have an outport at Lunenburg or Liverpool, 75 or 100 miles away from Halifax, than to have one 300 or 400 or 500 miles away in some other province.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
While Deep Brook in Digby county, where there is a very considerable development in process of construction, is in the constituency of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley), I am bound to say, and I ought to say in justice to him, that not on a single occasion did the Minister of Finance ask that that development be placed there. The Deep Brook development and every other development that has taken place in eastern Canada, in western Canada, or in any other part of the world for that matter, have been undertaken on the advice and with the approval of the technical advisers of the department for naval services, the chief of naval staff, and his subordinates.
I can assure my hon. friend the member for St. John-Albert that it is not a matter of the Minister of Transport failing in his duty or of the Minister of Finance having an excess of zeal. That is not the way the department for naval services is run. Neither gentlemen has made representations to me, either for the province of Nova Scotia or for the province of New Brunswick. Each of them has taken the correct course and said, "Let those undertakings, those buildings and wharves and whatever else is needed in the way of naval development be placed where they can best serve the war effort." That is the stand that these gentlemen have taken, and I think it is a sounder stand than this attempt to total up figures showing that Nova Scotia has received {29,000,000 in the way of land and buildings and New Brunswick, {19,000. Alberta and Saskatchewan, those inland provinces, obviously cannot share to the same extent as the coastal provinces, if that is to be the basis. The only possible way in which they might share would be in the operation of two buildings in each province, where the naval volunteer divisions would be housed. They can have no wharves, no breakwaters, no marine railways or dry docks. So that I repeat that to attempt to divide this dominion into certain zones, to reckon up the money spent in each and to say that because not so much has been spent here as there, therefore there is something wrong with the attitude of the department for naval services, I think is an incorrect stand to take.
Then my hon. friend asked about certain contracts contemplated in the province of New Brunswick, particularly I think in and around the city of Saint John. The hon. gentleman knows that in a certain part of northern New Brunswick, at an inland point, there is quite an extensive development in the way of a magazine. At Coverdale, near
Moncton, a contract has been let at a cost of 3141,000, for a barracks and station. I think the hon. gentleman asked for the name of the contractors; in this case they are the firm of Forbes and Sloat. * A contract has been let also at Saint John, New Brunswick, for the construction of certain buildings for the naval station at a cost of $329,000. That contract was awarded to M. A. Condon and Son on May 29. I might add that there has been some little difficulty in getting that work started, because one of the properties necessary to be had in order to erect these buildings has been very difficult to obtain. There has been difficulty in reaching any agreement with the owners, and probably it will be necessary for the department to take expropriation proceedings. In addition, plans are being prepared for the construction of an annex or addition to the present volunteer divisional quarters on Prince William street. I think all that building will be leased with the exception of the lower floor and perhaps the sub-basement, and some property adjoining will be obtained from the Canadian National railways on which will be erected a drill shed and sleeping quarters for the housing of approximately 130 men. In addition, certain mooring buoys will be laid in the harbour of Saint John which I think when in position will cost something over $100,000.
My hon. friend then went on to ask about travel and transportation, whether men are given free transportation when they are on leave, and I think he particularly inquired about men who return from foreign service, such as service in the Mediterranean. I may tell the hon. gentleman that men who return from foreign service are given free transportation, according to Canadian naval regulations. My hon. friend has asked whether the whole amount estimated for travel and transportation will be spent in Canada; whether it is all for railway travel, or whether some is for air and water travel, and how much in each case. 1 can say to my hon. friend that this amount provides for travel by rail, air and water. At the moment I cannot give him an analysis showing the amounts to be spent for travel on or in each of these elements. He wanted also to know which companies received the money paid for transportation. The amounts paid for railway transportation have been divided between the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway. For travel the Canadian National received $1,499,000 and the Canadian Pacific $1,167,000; for freight, the Canadian National, $773,000, and

War Appropriation-Naval Services
the Canadian Pacific, $119,000; for express, the Canadian National, $151,000, and the Canadian Pacific, $23,000.
Then my hon. friend wanted to know if the insurance principle applied to men serving in Canada or the waters thereof. My hon. friend the Minister of Pensions and National Health directed my attention to section 2, paragraph (o) (iii) of the act, which provides:
in the case of the naval, military or air forces during the war with the German reich, service on the high seas, in the field or in the air in any place outside Canada; or service in Canada, in such coastal or inland waters, or in such localities, whether in the field or in the air, as may from time to time be designated by the governor in council. . . .
-shall be considered to be service in a theatre of actual war. Therefore I should say that a member of the Canadian naval service injured or killed in the coastal waters of Canada, on board a Canadian ship of war, would come under the application of the so-called insurance principle.
To return to the question about naval information, the particulars of which I now have under my hand, I may tell the hon. member for St. John-Albert that the civilian staff of the directorate includes the director himself and seven female clerks and stenographers. The director receives a salary of $4,500 a year and expenses. In the last year, which was not a complete year, his living expenses amounted to $56S and his travelling expenses to $95. The other members of the civilian staff are paid according to the civil service schedule. The total salaries of these others for the last fiscal year amounted to $10,523. The uniformed personnel of the directorate are as follows:
In British Columbia, Lieutenant Tate, who is in uniform and receives the pay and allowances of his rank.
In Ontario, Lieutenant Commander Strange; Lieutenant G. Richardson; Lieutenant Phillip Lee; Lieutenant K. Fosberry; Lieutenant J. Trepanier; Sub-Lieutenant Newton; Acting-Lieutenant Fyfe; Sub-Lieutenant Burwash and Sub-Lieutenant Willis, all of whom are in Ontario, and receive the pay and allowances of their rank.	In addition there are two
"Wrens", members of the Women's Royal Canadian Naval Service, who are employed at information headquarters in Ottawa.
In Nova Scotia there are Acting-Lieutenant Commander G. A. Lawrence and Lieutenant W. Slater, who receive the pay of their rank.
In Newfoundland is Lieutenant Shaw, who receives the pay of his rank.
In the United Kingdom are Lieutenant Commander Bartlett, Sub-Lieutenant McRitchie

and Sub-Lieutenant Keate, all of whom receive the pay of their rank.
I believe those are all the questions asked by the hon. member for St. John-Albert, although I believe he has some to ask later on.
Then, dealing with the question asked by the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains: The hon. member raised the question of the closing of the St. Lawrence. May I say in the first place that the St. Lawrence is not closed to traffic. I must point out, however, that the eastern Atlantic ports of Canada are considerably nearer the United Kingdom than are the cities of Montreal and Quebec. There is a difference of some hundreds of miles in the distance between Montreal and Liverpool, for instance, and that between Halifax and Liverpool. And in a war, where we must traverse dangerous waters, the natural inclination is to shorten as greatly as possible the distance to be travelled by water. Consequently, in some cases at any rate, it is desirable to have a larger proportion of shipments from Canada leaving eastern Atlantic ports than would otherwise be the case. Furthermore, ships can make more trips by sailing from Halifax to United Kingdom ports and back again, than they could if they sailed from Montreal. There is a quicker turnaround, as it is called in shipping circles.
But there is no question that traffic will be moving in the St. Lawrence, perhaps not in as great volume as in certain other years, but nevertheless in very considerable volume.
Then, the hon. member for Yale asked about expenditures for capital assistance, and wanted to know why this should be charged to the navy, as was indicated in a return tabled last year. I have not any recollection of the particular return the hon. member has in mind, but I may say it is not the practice to charge capital assistance to the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. Such assistance is provided by the Department of Munitions and Supply. It may be, however, that under the item of equipment and components in last year's estimates something was charged to the Department of National Defence for Naval Services. Whether that was done incorrectly, I am not sure; but I can tell my hon. friend that that practice is not continuing.
Then, a question was asked as to the age at which the boys may leave sea cadet units. Sea cadet regulations provide that the ages shall be between twelve and eighteen years. I understand that certain corps in different parts of the country have their own ideas about age limits. Some are inclined to admit the boys immediately upon their reaching the

War Appropriation-Naval Services
age of twelve years, while others feel the boys should not be admitted until they are fourteen or fifteen years old. Some, I believe, want the boys to leave at the age of seventeen years instead of eighteen. That is a matter in respect of which there is some leeway allowed the corps. But the regulations do provide that boys may remain in the corps until they reach the age of eighteen, at which time they are old enough to join the Royal Canadian Navy. I may tell my hon. friend there is no>
entry into the Royal Canadian Navy at the moment for boy seamen, and I do not think there have been any entries since the beginning of the war.
Then, the hon. member wanted to know whether we have something in Canada like the royal naval benevolent trust. We have the royal Canadian naval benevolent fund. Whether it is exactly like the royal navy trust, I cannot say. No contribution is required from the men in connection with our fund, but a certain amount of unclaimed prize money, and certain other moneys contributed by various naval canteens have been put into the fund, which now amounts to a good many thousands of dollars, and which sum has been invested carefully, mostly I believe in victory bonds.

I
think the prize fund is a carry-over from the last war. This unclaimed prize money, together with certain other funds, including canteen funds, some time after the beginning of this war was put into the Royal Canadian Navy benevolent fund. I understand from the authorities of the fund that nothing has been paid out, and that during the war it may not be necessary to pay any out. After the war, when men may find themselves in somewhat straitened circumstances, the real need for the fund may be felt.
Then, the hon. member asked a question about the air officer commanding at Halifax, and whether he was under the naval commander in chief. That is a difficult question to answer. The title of Admiral Murray, the naval officer, is that of Commander-inChief, Canadian Northwest Atlantic. The title of the air officer is that of Air Officer Commanding. I should think that without any great argument between the two of them as to seniority they will get along very
well, Admiral Murray taking general charge of all anti-submarine activity, and the air officer taking charge of air activities over the sea.
Then the hon. member asked about Squadron Leader Desloges, who has been given certain duties in the St. Lawrence area. I can say that Squadron Leader Desloges is not in charge of any naval force. He is more in the nature of a liaison officer between the armed services- the navy, air and army-on the one hand, and the civilian defence corps, provincial police and other civilian services of that sort on the other.
The next question was with reference to categories on enlistment. We have certain people who are not fit for general duty but who are able to undertake certain other duties. We now have a special branch which employs some men who are not fit for sea duty for one reason or another. Then there is a shore branch where we employ sailmakers, blacksmiths and the like. We take them in up to sixty years of age, which is far beyond the age which would entitle them to enter for sea service.

I have asked for some information on that, but I am sorry I have not received it. Perhaps I should not attempt to reply before I get it. My impression is that there are no deductions except where an income tax might be exigible, which would not happen in many cases, and such deductions as a man might make to his wife and so on. I will make sure on that point and let my hon. friend know to-morrow.
I wish to thank the hon. member for

War Appropriation-Naval Services
Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) and other members who have been kind enough to speak well of the Canadian navy and the work it is doing. I want also to say a word, perhaps not quite in the same spirit, about the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Church). In spite of what the hon. member said this afternoon and this evening about his great friendship for me personally and his great regard for the navy, it is difficult for me to reconcile these statements with others he has made from time to time in this house. My hon. friend's references to the Canadian navy go back a good many years.
In 1926 the house was discussing the procedure to be followed1 in ratifying treaties. The question was whether the procedure which had been recommended by the imperial conference of 1923 should be adopted by the parliament of Canada. The hon. member for Broadview-at that time he represented Toronto North West-took a very strong stand on the matter. He said that Sir John A. Macdonald1 had been satisfied with the status of Canada; that the soldiers who had died in France and Flanders were satisfied with it, and then he went on to say, as reported1 at page 4787 of Hansard:
Talk about Canada being independent, . . . Why if we were independent a foreign fleet might sail up the St. Lawrence and we would not have as much as a rowboat to oppose it because our toy navy is locked up in a garage at Halifax.
Two years later, the hon. member was speaking on February 1, 1928, and is reported at pages 103 and 104 of Hansard as follows:
We have a contemptible little navy which hugs the shores, never leaves our coasts and for the past year has been locked up in a garage at Halifax.
Then he went on, as reported at page 106-

Then I come to the Department of National Defence.

The minister of this department is also actively engaged in putting the Liberal party on the map, and the returned men off the map. I suppose he intends to unlock the door of the garage at Halifax and let our navy run up and

Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I have talked- and also thought-for nearly forty minutes. Not every member can think for that period of time. But I have only dealt with the fringe of my subject. speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I pass over the other years and come to 1940. On November 22 of that year the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) asked a question, as reported at pages 336 and 337 of Hansard, about the establishment of a naval college. The hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew) had been quoted in a newspaper as having stated that the naval college would be established on the Pacific coast, and the hon. member for Cumberland wished to know whether it was to be established there or in Nova Scotia. The hon. member for Broadview then leaped to his feet and asked me as Minister of National Defence for Naval Services if in the future, I would give information to the house about the establishment of such an institution before it was disclosed to the newspapers over the head and against the regular practice of parliament. I had made no statement whatever about the college except to say that no site had been selected. The hon. member for Broadview then asked if the British admiralty had been consulted, implying that we did not have the power to erect a naval college in Canada at the place and time we wished. He then went on with a very gratuitous jibe at an officer of the navy named Lieutenant Farrow, who had been director of publicity for the navy but who at that time I think was serving at sea with the Canadian navy. My hon. friend apparently never liked this officer for some reason or

War Appropriation-Naval Services
another, because he frequently asked questions about him, and his final compliment to the college was to say:
I suppose the minister will announce the appointment of Lieutenant Farrow as commandant of the college.
Then I turn to 1942, May 13. page 2391 of Hansard. There was some discussion that day about sinkings in the St. Lawrence. My hon. friend the member for Broadview said in a none too complimentary voice:
Where was your navy when all this was going on in the St. Lawrence?
Then on the 16th of July-I have not the exact date but it was about the middle of July, 1942-at a time when I was at a shipyard in Ontario which had been burned out with the loss of one ship and the partial loss of another, and when I was endeavouring to make arrangements with other shipbuilders around there to come to the assistance of this yard which has been destroyed, at that very moment when I was there the hon. member for Broadview asked some question in the house of the department for naval services. The Prime Minister replied that I would be back in a day or two and would answer it then, and my hon. friend's friendship for me manifested itself by saying:
He ought to be here.
I notice that my hon. friend is very rarely in his seat on Monday afternoon and for a good part of Friday afternoon, but when I was out trying to straighten out a shipyard in distress -I am glad to say that the boat builders rallied magnificently-that is the sort of thanks I get from the hon. member for Broadview.
