speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I am not going to deal with the point of order, Mr. Chairman, but should like to make one or two further references.
On the 17th of March of this year-if the hon. member for Bow River wants recent occurrences, this is one that happened this session-the hon. member for Broadview said:
Will the minister make a statement about the escort strength? We seem to have been trusting to Providence more than the Canadian navy.
This is the kind of statement by the hon. member for Broadview to which I object, and I say that I am not for one moment misled by statements such as he made this afternoon to the effect that he was a great friend of mine and of the Canadian navy and that he had urged rearmament for the last twenty years, because the statements I have just quoted indicate that he is not a friend certainly of the minister or of the minister who occupied the position of Minister of National Defence some fifteen years ago.
My hon. friend asked a further question this afternoon. It was a complaint rather than a question, and the gist of it was that the enlisted man in Canada loses his civilian status whereas in Britain, Australia and New Zealand he retains it, and has all the rights of protection based on the liberty of the subject. He went on to indicate that the enlisted man in Canada lost. those rights and could not even write to his own member of parliament if he had a complaint to make. I tried to correct my hon. friend at the time, but the leader of the opposition became very technical and did not want any interruptions. I wanted to tell the hon. member for Broadview that I was not aware of any difference whatever between the rules governing the Canadian serviceman and the serviceman in Great Britain. In fact I knew that all our King's Regulations and Admiralty Instructions for the army, navy and air force were based and drawn very largely upon the regulations in force in Great Britain for the particular service. I am supported in that by section 13 of King's Regulations and Admiralty Instructions, which reads as follows:
No person in the fleet is to enter into direct communication with any service or department of the state or with any subordinate officer of such service or department, at home or abroad, on subjects connected with the naval service or with his particular duties or present or future employment, unless authorized to do so by the regulations of the service or superior authority; but all communications on such subjects are to be made through the proper channels to the admiralty or to the commanders in chief abroad, in order that such steps may be taken therein as may be necessary.

War Appropriation-Naval Services
That I interpret to mean quite clearly that a man in the fleet in Great Britain is not at complete liberty to write at any time he wishes to anybody to whom he wishes to write, but is bound and controlled by this article of the King's Regulations and Admiralty Instructions, and that is exactly the same article which governs and- controls the actions of Canadian sailors.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as I represent the constituency, bordering on the gulf of St. Lawrence, where we suffered heavy losses in ships during the past year, I was pleased to hear the statement which the Prime Minister made to the house this afternoon regarding the policy which the government proposes to adopt with a view to ensure better protection to the gulf this year.
When I fought last year, as the committee no doubt remembers, for improvements in our protection system, I was sure, as a result of the disasters which had unfortunately occurred in the gulf, that the three branches of the national defence, could, under better leadership, and with closer cooperation, afford us more efficient protection; I was sure that we were exposed to serious dangers in that connection and that our area was the one where the enemy menace was the greatest.
I have no doubt that the population scattered on the shores of the river and the gulf will generously support the fulfilment of that defence programme, and, if need be, help to preserve the integrity of our national territory, even if it should entail the greatest sacrifices. Besides, those people had realized long ago that the situation was fraught with serious dangers. I was sure, when I discussed those matters in the house and was confronted with opposition on all sides, that I was voicing such fears, which have clearly stood out in the Charlevoix-Saguenay election.
Our people knew that had the battle of the Atlantic taken a more favourable turn for the enemy, the latter could easily have driven an attack inland through that wide open gateway.
For those reasons, I was glad to hear the statement of the policy which the government proposes to adopt in order to afford to that part of our country a better protection which, undoubtedly, will give very good results and restore confidence in the minds of the people.
In conclusion, I wish to express the hope that during the present navigation season, with all those protective measures and the general support of the civil population of Gaspe, we shall not have to deplore disasters like those which occurred last year.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
In the first place I wish to congratulate very sincerely the hon. member for Vegreville and the hon. member for St. John-Albert, who spoke very well this afternoon. I could not be here all the time, but I listened to their speeches with deep interest, and what they said was worthy of note. With regard to the hon. member for Broadview, I do not think the minister is right in giving him the cold shoulder when he showed such a friendly disposition.
This afternoon I listened with great attention to the Prime Minister while he read his statement. It is an important statement because it recognized the valiant and courageous efforts in this chamber of the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Roy), and it was also a recognition of the true significance of the byelection in which the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) was returned last fall. For a time the hon. member for Gaspe was almost alone in bringing to the attention of the government matters of defence, not only of the territory he represents here, but of the whole country; and although he has not been given all that he asked, I give credit to the government for admitting that it is a pressing matter and that something should be done. What was mentioned by the Prime Minister this afternoon was the civilian defence, the extension of the aircraft detection; also he said that planes would be in readiness and telephone lines would be open for urgent calls.
The purpose of the mobilization act was one month of training, extended to all, and if I remember what was said to me at the time, the idea was to have a force disseminated throughout the country in order to repel any invasion by an enemy. The late Mr. Lapointe, and the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), who was then a member of the cabinet, spoke on this line, and the fall of France made possible an attack from Germany or some other enemy. It meant that after the fall of France this country was more exposed to invasion, and therefore men should be on the spot ready to repel invasion. Well, afterwards it was changed and now we have recourse to civilian defence. But if the Pulhems system is put into force, and if the army keeps not only the physically fit men, but all the others, placed in different categories, who will form the civilian defence?
The minister said that defence should not be organized on the same lines as public works, which are distributed throughout the country.
I agree with him to a certain extent; but on the other hand, if our country is exposed, where will be the invasion if we are to be invaded by an enemy? No one knows. I

War Appropriation-Naval Services
hope that this country will not be invaded, but if the enemy decides to come here, where will he attack? No one knows. In the United States there is coast protection from Maine South to Florida, and as the minister well knows, they have 700,000 volunteers who search the sky for aeroplanes and have powerful projectors operating in the sky, on the sea and on the land. They do things very well there, and, even though we may not wish to follow all that is done in the United States, there are examples which it would be wise for us to follow.	_
There is another consideration. It is, that when the Canadian people show good will with regard to enlistments, as they do in my county, and with regard to subscriptions to victory loans, the amounts of which were always oversubscribed, although incomes are much reduced, it has to be taken into consideration, and these fellows want to see the colour of the money, not to derive any personal benefit but to be assured of reasonable protection. If we tell Canadian citizens, "this country is well defended," and then we add, "Look around and see if you are satisfied with it," and they see nothing, the answer is clear. They are not satisfied. They want adequate protection.
There must be cooperation between the three branches of the armed forces. The minister represents the naval services; there is also the air defence and the militia; and all three should work together. We need camps at different places. It is a mistake to have camps which are too large; it is good to have camps disseminated throughout the country. I have been insisting for a long time that there should be a training centre at Riviere du Loup; it is a much better place than even Montmagny or Rimouski. One camp was established at Montmagny, thirty miles from Quebec city, and the other one at Rimouski. Why should there be a camp at Riviere du Loup? For this simple reason, that there is close connection between the St. Lawrence river and the United States throughout the county of Temiscouata from north to south, and it is an old military route. It was built by the Royal Engineers at the time of the Fenian raid, and when the minister or any minister speaks, of modern experts he might bear in mind that this road was built by experts who had as much knowledge of military business as those of to-day, if not more. It was to connect the United States and Canada. Very often I have asked the Minister of National Defence to see to it that that route is broadened and rebuilt to be serviceable for military purposes, and I have
always been listened to with a deaf ear. _ I am not referring in this connection to the minister for naval services.
In case of invasion, if it comes to the east, this is the nearest approach by road and rail from the United States. It is a small railway which operates there, but we need improvements to that highway and they should be carried out by the defence department. For three or four years, in fact for many years, I have been advocating that. I took it up with the Minister of Labour before the war. The present Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) can see the memoranda which I sent to his predecessor, who was afterwards Minister of National Defence and who died too early. I am sure that if the Hon. Mr. Rogers had lived a little longer, that route would1 have been widened and rebuilt by his own department.
That route is essential because, if this country becomes a theatre of war; if the enemy comes here, the railways may not be sufficient to transport all that we need. We may need transport by truck and, in fact, when there are military trucks that go to Halifax or Saint John, they pass over that highway, route No. 2. Now there is very little tourist traffic, and I suggest that it is time to do that work and to see to it that we have every facility extended to us for the improvement of our defence.
The third point is that we need some navy boats on the river at Riviere du Loup. The nearest point is Rimouski, a distance of sixty miles. Riviere du Loup is in front of the Saguenay river on the opposite shore of the river, and it would form a good base for some boats. Besides that, we have a naval college in the province of Quebec at St. Hyacinthe near a muddy river, a river in which there is very little water. There is more mud than water. I do not see why such a college is not near the St. Lawrence river. We shall need also an airport and some men to protect the railways and the railway approaches and bridges. That means that a great deal will have to be done, but it cannot be done by the civilian protection alone. It needs the cooperation of all men of good-will, who are ready to admit that eastern Canada is a part of Canada. That is all we want. I have been insisting on that year after year. Never, however, did I have a favourable report. I succeeded in having the engineer of the Department of Transport come to Temiscouata county in 1940, but he came early in the spring when the roads and the fields were covered with snow and it was hard to find a proper location for an airport. I do not see why that part of Canada should not be

War Appropriation-Naval Services
entitled to an airport. It would afford excellent facilities to all Royal Canadian Air Force men who come to that district.
The defence of this country will not be effected by order in council; it must be carried out on the spot. There are things that appeal to common sense, things which cannot be denied. They must be admitted. Our people are willing to do their share and they are doing it very well, but they need that protection to which they are entitled as Canadian citizens.
Again I congratulate very warmly the hon. member for Gaspe upon what he has done in the past, and I am ready to admit that in very large part what has been decided is due to his painstaking efforts. I also congratulate the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay upon his election, which was an eye-opener. Let me assure the minister that I do not approach this question of defence from any parochial point of view, but I want the country well defended. When my hon. friends from British Columbia argued their case-and they did it very well- I supported them, and I am ready to support any request they make for their part of the country. On the other hand, we want their support for eastern Canada as well. I hope that the fears which have been entertained, and which were justified to a large extent, will not materialize and that the enemy will not come to our shores. But the fact is that the enemy came within the St. Lawrence river, and I hope that the order in council which was read this afternoon was not passed simply to appease eastern Canadians who were not satisfied with the way in which the defence was organized in past years.
In conclusion, there are two questions I wish to ask the minister. There are interchangeable heads in the defence department, and I understand that the Minister of National Defence is first of the war ministers and that the minister for air is his associate. I wonder if the minister for naval services has something to do with the other two departments. If so,
I would be thankful if he would say what it is.
There is another thing. Some time ago it was mentioned in the press that there would be ten parliamentary assistants. Some of them have been appointed. I do not know the number, but I do know that there are not ten.
I should like to know something about this without having any names mentioned. One of our colleagues has been mentioned as assistant to the minister and he is very worthy of that honour, if I may so describe it. He could discharge the duties very well. I wonder why the minister does not have a parliamentary

assistant just as there are parliamentary assistants for the Minister of National Defence and the Minister of National Defence for Air. The Minister for Naval Services may say that his budget is less than the budgets of the others. That is true, but his budget this year is as much as the whole of the civil estimates in a year before the war. I wonder if the minister will not have a parliamentary assistant in the near future. I do not wish him to disclose the name of the one who will be chosen.
Mr. GRAYDON.* Does the hon. member think it will be the hon. member for Broadview?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
It could have been possible until the minister spoke, because the hon. member for Broadview was in a very friendly mood, but I do not know what will be his disposition following the words of the minister. Let me tell the minister something else in regard to the hon. member for Broadview and himself. This discussion is not a matter of friendship; it is not a matter of saying, "After you, my dear Alphonse; after you, my dear Gaston," It is a matter of very serious business; it is the very serious matter of the defence of this country. Sometimes we may disagree with the minister, but there is no man more broad-minded than the hon. member for Broadview. While I often disagree with him on public matters, I have the highest regard for the hon. gentleman, and I can say that he is one of my very best friends. One has only to go to Toronto to see how popular he is with everyone, particularly with the underprivileged man about whom no one thinks.
The matter is very simple. The minister cannot expect hon. members to discuss such serious matters, matters of life and death, from, a sentimental point of view. I am against sentiment in war. We must be matter of fact; we must get down to brass tacks; we must see to it that the country suffers as little as possible. The minister occupies an important post but, like all of us, he is only a man and a man can make mistakes. Because mistakes are made at times; because a member makes some remarks that may not please at the time, he should not be considered unfriendly. Having said that, Mr. Chairman, I hope the minister will take my remarks into consideration, for I shall have to repeat them when the bill is under consideration if no progress is made in regard to the matters I have mentioned.

War Appropriation-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
My hon. friend has asked two questions. The first was whether I have anything to do with the other two departments of defence. The statute provides that if one minister of defence is absent, one of the two remaining ministers acts in his behalf and with his authority, while, if two are absent, the remaining minister acts in behalf of those two. Otherwise the positions are not interchangeable. Of course there is very full consultation between the three defence ministers; at meetings of defence council, which are also attended by the chiefs of staff and the deputy ministers, and again at meetings of the war committee of the cabinet, which are attended by the three defence ministers as well as the Prime Minister and certain other members of the government.
The second question was why no parliamentary assistant has been appointed. My hon. friend knows very well that with such a tremendous surplus of excellent material on this side of the house, including the hon. member for Temiscouata, it is very difficult to select an assistant. I have not made any decision on the question as to who should be selected or whether anyone should be selected. Of course the matter is one for the Prime Minister as well as the minister directly concerned.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I regret to have to rise
to a question of privilege, Mr. Chairman. I understand that in my absence from the chamber to-night, after having offered some constructive criticism, the minister insulted me and the whole opposition. After all, the opposition have some rights in this honourable house, and I object to that sort of thing. I never said that I was a friend of the minister; I do not know him well enough to be a friend. All I have done is humbly to do my duty as a member of parliament, and I certainly have something to say about a spendthrift department like this. It should be put back where it was under the army; there was no necessity for the creation of this department. It has been nothing but a sink-hole for the country's money, half a billion dollars, and I object to it. I have taken a consistent stand in this house for rearmament, and I know no friends except it be my duty as a member of parliament. I do object to a new minister lecturing the committee in this way. I shall read his remarks in Hansard to-morrow morning and make my reply later.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: We shall await that with great interest; my hon. friend has plenty of time to prepare replies.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
I ask for a retraction by the minister, and I can tell him that I am going to discuss every item of his estimates.
I have no quarrel with him or his department at all, but I have contended that while there should be an air department there was no necessity for the creation of this department, the expenditures of which are going up by leaps and bounds. I do wish to follow along the line of the remarks of the hon. member for Temiscouata, but the Toronto Star has published another report in regard to the speeches made in this house. I have not occupied one-half the time they said. I have discussed public affairs here fairly and squarely, in a decent and honourable manner;
I have made no attacks upon the government or upon any minister. I have done my duty in this house as a gentleman, and I do not intend to be lectured by a newcomer from the maritime provinces. That may go in the Nova Scotia legislature, but so far as I am concerned it will not go another day in this house. The minister represents a constituency in Ontario, but so far as I can see Ontario has not been given fair treatment.
I have no wish to further take part in this debate. I believe I have done my duty as a member of parliament in calling the attention of the house and the country to these expenditures. I have supported rearmament; I have supported the navy; I have supported the action that has been taken by the govern^ ment. I do not seek any quarrel with the minister. He is a newcomer; all I know about him is what I see of him over there, but he has no business to make remarks about me in my absence. I never said I was a friend of his. A member of parliament must do his duty. Criticism is a tonic which stirs governments to action, and, so far as I can see, the only action we have had has come as a result of criticism from this side of the house. I know no friendship except my duty to the returned men, and I do regret that personalities should enter into this debate. This is no place for them; this conflict is too serious for matters of that description. The minister has so many press agents who infest the newspaper offices that I fail to see where we are getting value for the money, and I am only one member of the opposition.
It is eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I do not wish to offer any further criticism, but I can only repeat that I have no quarrel with the minister at all, and no desire except to do my duty.
Progress reported.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
